title: Dangerous mosquito-borne virus spreads in one state as officials warn of rising cases
summary: Florida dengue fever cases hit 41 statewide as mosquito-control crews ramp up aerial spraying and inspections across Tampa Bay's hardest-hit counties.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, discusses the spread, symptoms and management of West Nile virus.

Florida mosquito-control agencies are stepping up surveillance, inspections and spraying, as officials expect the number of locally acquired dengue fever cases in Tampa Bay and across the state to rise in the coming weeks.
As of Sept. 1, the number of dengue fever cases originating in Florida this year had climbed to 33 in Tampa Bay and 41 statewide. Cases are predicted to increase, Fox 13 Tampa Bay reported.
Locally acquired cases mean people contracted the illness where they live rather than while traveling abroad.
DEADLY MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS CLAIMS FIRST LIFE IN MAJOR US CITY AS CASES SPREAD
The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) reported 30 confirmed cases in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County.
Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health.
Florida mosquito-control agencies are increasing surveillance, inspections and spraying as the state reports dozens of locally acquired dengue cases. (iStock)

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The virus is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hawaii has recorded past outbreaks, and the virus is common in the U.S. territories of Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and American Samoa.
The CDC reported in May that 2024 was a record year for dengue in the U.S.
Removing standing water around homes can help eliminate breeding sites for mosquitoes that can transmit dengue. (iStock)

A total of 3,798 cases were reported from U.S. states and the District of Columbia, a 359% increase over the annual average for 2010 through 2023. About 97% of those cases were travel-associated, and roughly 3% were locally acquired.

Florida reported the most dengue cases among U.S. states and Washington, D.C., in 2024, with 1,044 cases, or more than a quarter of the total. Florida recorded 85 locally acquired cases across 10 counties that year, compared with 18 in California and two in Texas.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro told Fox 13.

"The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission."
Florida mosquito-control agencies are increasing surveillance, inspections and spraying as the state reports dozens of locally acquired dengue cases. (iStock)
Stopping the spread

Mosquito-control crews in Florida are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to local reports.

FMCA is urging residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The FMCA also advises people to follow what it calls the "three Ds."

Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.Dump standing water from containers around the home, and check yards regularly.
Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.
Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.
Dump standing water from containers around the home, and check yards regularly.
Health officials urge residents in areas with dengue transmission to take precautions to avoid mosquito bites. (iStock)
Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic.
In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness.
People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Longevity doctor reveals what matters most for aging well, beyond pricey biohacks
summary: Dr. Annu Navani shares four low-cost longevity habits rooted in sleep, stress management, nutrition and resistance training for a longer health span.
story: Dr. Annu Navani, chief medical officer at Le Reve Wellness, revelas why people should focus on adding healthy years to life — not chasing immortality.

As "biohacks" like peptides, cold plunges and high-tech wearables grow in popularity, some advocates promote the idea of dramatically extending human life — but others say it’s better to focus on more healthy years rather than living forever.

Dr. Annu Navani — chief medical officer at Le Reve Wellness in San Jose, California, where she leads advanced regenerative and longevity medicine programs — said the biggest myth is that people will be able to live for a "very, very long period of time."

"I do feel we have extended the human lifespan to some extent," Navani, who is also founder of the World Institute of Regenerative Medicine, told Fox News Digital. "So yes, we are making progress, but I think it would be a false promise if we said people would live beyond 120 or 130 years of life."
ARE PEPTIDES THE FOUNTAIN OF YOUTH? DOCTORS WARN HYPE MAY OUTPACE SCIENCE
Instead, Navani said the goal should be to improve the quality of the years people have.
"Longevity medicine is all about adding life to those years, not so much years to life," she said.
A longevity doctor says the goal should be improving the quality of the years people have rather than trying to "live forever." (iStock)
4 longevity habits that won't break the bank
Longevity medicine does not necessarily have to mean costly procedures, supplements or biohacks, according to Navani.
For those who have limited time or money, the doctor recommends "starting from within the daily routines of smart practices."
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Navani shared the following four pillars of health that form the foundation of longevity, all of which "don't cost much money at all."
"I think sleep is really understated in terms of its importance for overall health and longevity," she said.
"Studies have shown that at least seven hours of sleep is [generally recommended] for a human being to be able to perform optimally, and has been linked to a good life and a decent health lifespan."
"I think sleep is really understated in terms of its importance and overall health and longevity," the doctor said. (iStock)
The CDC's guidance recommends seven or more hours for adults, but individual sleep needs vary.
Navani recommends eating at least three or four hours before bed, avoiding stimulating activities such as laptop use, and practicing calming routines like meditation, gratitude or journaling.
Health agencies recommend managing stress through a combination of physical activity, optimal sleep, relaxation techniques, proper nutrition and social connections.
Navani said she begins her day with 20 minutes of meditation and gratitude, which helps calm her mind and relieve stress.
DEMENTIA RISK COULD BE TIED TO YOUR MINDSET AND OUTLOOK ON LIFE, STUDY SUGGESTS
She also recommends meditating in the evening as a way to unwind before bed.

General dietary guidance recommends building meals around a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins, and low-fat or fat-free dairy, while limiting added sugars, saturated fat and sodium.
A balanced eating pattern should also be tailored to a person’s age, health needs and preferences, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s guidance.

General dietary guidance recommends building meals around a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins and low-fat or fat-free dairy, while limiting added sugars, saturated fat and sodium. (iStock)
The CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity — or 75 minutes of vigorous activity — plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days per week.
Navani identified high-intensity resistance training as her pick for the most important habit for people in their 50s and beyond.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Studies have shown how it builds bone health and helps musculoskeletal blood flow," she said. "Muscle strength and muscle resilience are linked to health span and longevity, as they impact cardiovascular and neurovascular health."
Navani also identified VO₂ max — which is the maximum amount of oxygen the body can use during intense exercise — as an important marker of overall health and longevity.
The doctor identified high-intensity resistance training as the most important habit for people in their 50s and beyond. (iStock)
"I think VO₂ max is a really important key biomarker that has been shown in quite a few studies to be linked positively to good health and longer lifespan," she said.
The metric is widely used as a measure of cardiorespiratory fitness, reflecting how efficiently the heart, lungs and muscles work together.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For some older adults or people with health conditions, lower-intensity or supervised strength training may be more appropriate, experts say.
Navani emphasized that it’s never too late to meaningfully improve health span.
"I often say if you didn't start in your 20s, the best time to start is today," she said. "I have a lot of patients who come to me when they are 55 and 60 and we start the journey then."
One-hour kickstart
The longevity doctor shared her own simple morning routine that she follows to kick-start each day, which includes breaking the first hour of the day into three 20-minute segments.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The first segment focuses on meditation and gratitude.
"The first 20 minutes is just meditating and waking up and kind of just being grateful and thankful," she shared. "That helps calm me down and relieves stress."
Dr. Annu Navani emphasized that it’s never too late to meaningfully improve health span.  (Fox News Digital)
The second 20-minute segment is devoted to movement, which includes stretching, exercising and resistance training.
The final 20 minutes are reserved for reading, she said: "I read something that I really want to capture in my brain, something I want to remember."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Navani advised against immediately reaching for the phone or opening email first thing in the morning, instead recommending using that time to read something intellectually engaging.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Why Tasers sometimes fail to stop suspects — and what weight has to do with it
summary: Multiple Taser deployments failed to stop Pamela Cisneros in the Times Square stabbing, raising urgent questions about how body composition can impact effectiveness.
story: Fox News' Todd Piro provides details on an incident in Times Square after a woman armed with kitchen knives stabbed two people, killing one. NYPD officers reportedly deployed tasers before shooting the suspect.

Multiple Taser deployments failed to stop Pamela Cisneros, 49, during a roughly four-minute standoff in Times Square last Monday, after she allegedly stabbed two people. The attack left a 32-year-old woman dead and a 68-year-old man wounded.

"As multiple officers discharged Tasers, which proved to be ineffective, the subject continued to advance toward our officers with the knives," Jessica Tisch, New York City police commissioner, said in a news conference that evening.

When the Tasers failed to subdue Cisneros — who stated, "I’m not dropping anything. I would rather kill both of you" — two officers opened fire, striking her. Cisneros was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
NYPD IDENTIFIES WOMAN KILLED IN TIMES SQUARE STABBING SPREE
The incident sparked broader questions about why Tasers sometimes fail and whether obesity or body composition can impede their effectiveness.
The recent incident on Times Square sparked broader questions about why Tasers sometimes fail and whether obesity or body composition can impede their effectiveness. (iStock)
A standard Taser is designed to fire two small, barbed probes connected to the device by insulated, conductive wires, according to Axon, the manufacturer.

"Electrical pulses travel along those wires and into the body, triggering involuntary muscle contractions," Axon’s website states. "For NMI to occur, it is best that two probes make contact 12 inches (30 cm) or more apart."
"Your large muscle masses are your back and thighs. Officers are trained to aim for those areas."

Steve Keller, a retired police sergeant in Blue Ash, Ohio, said the most common causes of Taser failure include clothing, probe placement, substance abuse by the perpetrator and connectivity between probes.
However, obesity can affect the Taser, he said, as a large layer of body fat could interfere with the connectivity.
Multiple Taser deployments failed to stop Pamela Cisneros, 49, during a roughly four-minute standoff in Times Square last Monday, after she allegedly stabbed two people. (Fox 5)
"The purpose of the Taser is neuromuscular in capacity," Keller told Fox News Digital.

"Your large muscle masses are your back and thighs. Officers are trained to aim for those areas," he said, just as they are also trained to adjust their aiming for clothing and the distance between them and the subject.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
If one of the probes hits the abdomen and the person is obese, it can affect the connectivity of the two probes, according to Keller.
"If one probe hits the person and the other probe misses, the Taser will not work," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
For example, if one probe hits a subject in the thigh and the other probe hits a thick bubble jacket, there’s a good chance the officer won’t have good connectivity, Keller said.
The incident sparked broader questions about why Tasers sometimes fail and whether obesity or body composition can impede their effectiveness. (Fox 5)
"The same could be considered if there is a large layer of body fat — they could still feel it, but it might not be as effective."
Referring to Cisneros’ case, Keller emphasized that mental health may also play a significant role in how a person responds to a Taser.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Tisch confirmed at the press conference that the suspect had a documented mental health history with the NYPD, with one incident in 2018 and another in 2019.
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, agreed that body composition can affect the Taser’s effectiveness.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Tasers are much more effective for muscle than fat because muscle conducts electricity much better, and the Taser delivers a high voltage," he said. "In an obese person, it is more difficult to find an area that conducts electricity."
Fox News Digital reached out to Axon, the NYPD and obesity organizations requesting comment.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Georgia woman celebrates 112th birthday, reveals her secret to a long life
summary: Mabel Dunbar of Fayetteville, Georgia, turned 112 and says religious faith and close family ties are the secrets behind her remarkable longevity.
story: Dr. Jessica Gray explains several factors contributing to the increase in U.S. life expectancy, including decreased drug overdoses and improved cancer survival rates.
A Georgia woman who just celebrated her 112th birthday credits her longevity to staying close to her family and embracing her strong religious faith.

Mabel Dunbar, of Fayetteville, Georgia, was born in Jamaica in 1914. She is the mother of one, grandmother of four and a great-grandmother, and was honored by loved ones on her birthday Sept. 5 with a custom berry cake, flowers and a crown, FOX 5 Atlanta reported.
"God is love and I love my families," Dunbar said at her party. "I love all my families and strangers."
HOW A 93-YEAR-OLD SOCCER REFEREE CREDITS WARTIME RATIONS AND DISCIPLINE FOR HIS LONGEVITY
Fayetteville resident Mabel Dunbar reflects on reaching her 112th birthday milestone surrounded by loved ones at her metro Atlanta home on September 5, 2026. (FOX 5 Atlanta)
Those who know her describe Dunbar as "deeply religious, pleasant and talkative," according to FOX 5.

She spent her life serving others and remaining active, the station reported. Until recently, Dunbar still enjoyed cooking and made breakfast for herself every morning. She also enjoyed sharing stories with visitors.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
After moving to Florida to live with her daughter in 1994, Dunbar relocated to Fayetteville in August 2025 to live with her granddaughter and grandson-in-law.
Family remains an important part of Dunbar’s daily life, according to FOX 5.

"Treat them the best you can, because they are important," Dunbar said of younger generations, specifically her grandchildren. "You need them when you can't help yourself like me. These good people are on me all the time, and I'm happy to see them when they come."
A custom berry cake decorated for Mabel Dunbar’s 112th birthday milestone sits ready for family festivities in Fayetteville on September 5, 2026. (FOX 5 Atlanta)
Leading oncologist and University of Pennsylvania bioethicist Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel has identified several principles for living longer and reducing disease risk.

They include prioritizing an active social life, staying mentally active with new hobbies and opportunities to learn, limiting processed and sugary foods and drinks without being overly restrictive, engaging in moderate exercise and getting proper sleep, Fox News Digital previously reported.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Emanuel also recommends avoiding obviously dangerous activities and behaviors.
Religious involvement has also been associated with greater longevity, research has suggested.
Generations of family gather around 112-year-old Mabel Dunbar at her Fayetteville home to celebrate her long life and Jamaican heritage. (FOX 5 Atlanta)

In a 2016 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health examined religious service attendance and health outcomes among 74,534 women over 16 years.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
They found that women who attended religious services more than once a week had a 33% lower risk of dying during the follow-up period compared with women who never attended religious services.
Family members place a sparkling birthday crown on 112-year-old Mabel Dunbar during a milestone celebration at her Fayetteville home. (FOX 5 Atlanta)

Weekly attendance was associated with a 26% lower risk, while attendance less than once a week was associated with a 13% lower risk. Regular attendees also tended to smoke less, experience fewer depressive symptoms and have stronger social support, the researchers reported in 2016.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The world’s oldest documented living person is Ethel Caterham, of England, who turned 117 in August.
Caterham previously told The Associated Press that she credited her long life to "never arguing with anyone," adding, "I listen, and I do what I like."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Why couples should flirt with each other every day — plus the ‘red flag’ to avoid
summary: A relationship expert says flirting boosts self-esteem and confidence, but couples in long-term relationships often lose the "muscle memory" of playfulness.
story: Clinical sexologist Mindy DeSeta, PhD, shares how flirting can release dopamine and oxytocin, reduce stress and help people feel more confident, attractive and connected.
Flirting may do more than spark romantic interest — experts say it can also benefit emotional well-being, as long as it stays within appropriate boundaries.

Mindy DeSeta, Ph.D., a clinical sexologist and mental health counselor in Miami, Florida, defined flirting as a "one-on-one interpersonal experience," delivering a message that someone is interested in learning more about another person.
Flirting in general "feels good," the expert told Fox News Digital, adding that there are both emotional and physiological effects.
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
Flirting may activate brain chemicals involved in pleasure, reward and social bonding, DeSeta said. It can also lower the stress hormone cortisol.

"It builds confidence, it's a positive social interaction that improves self-esteem," she went on. "What I also hear is that people want to flirt in general because it makes them feel attractive and desired … That's a normal human feeling."
Flirting may activate brain chemicals involved in pleasure, reward and social bonding, experts said. (iStock)
DeSeta said she views flirting as a signal of attraction and believes it should remain between romantic partners or people pursuing a romantic relationship.
"It’s really hard to be platonic because it does release that bonding hormone," she said.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
For those who feel the need to flirt with someone who is not their partner, the expert suggested this could be a "red flag" for what’s happening in the relationship.
"As a sexologist, I'm a huge believer that we must date and flirt with our partner every day," DeSeta said.
Feeling the need to flirt with people outside your relationship may be a "red flag." (iStock)
It's normal for relationships to sometimes need a "reboot," she said.

"In one marriage, you're going to get many, many marriages… You'll find people getting stale or very hollow in their relationship, and that's when you will start looking outside to get those needs met, especially in flirting, because it's something that's very easy to do."
HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA
If flirting begins to extend beyond the relationship — from a coffee-shop barista to a colleague at the office — DeSeta advised stopping "immediately" and redirecting that energy toward the partner.

"Be vulnerable and go in with, ‘I miss this about us. I want to bring this back into our relationship,’" she said. "And don't forget to share, ‘This is what would make me feel attractive and desired by you.’"
When flirting fades

Anna Elton, Ph.D., a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said couples struggling with intimacy often miss the fun they shared at the beginning of their relationships.
"There’s a time and place for flirting, and you have to be in the right headspace."
As couples devote more attention to schedules, errands, bills and childcare, other aspects of the relationship can get pushed aside, Elton said.
Affection, physical touch, flirting and playfulness may become less frequent, making room for "stress, conflict and growing resentment."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Body changes, aging and stress can also affect how confident or desirable people feel, Elton noted.
"When couples have been together for a long time, I ask them, ‘So, how do you flirt with your partner? How do you let them know about your erotic intentions?’ And they say, ‘Oh, we don’t flirt.’"
Creating a "new language of flirting" can help couples reconnect and spark intimacy, Elton said.
Creating a "new language of flirting" can help spice up the relationship and spark moments of intimacy, experts say. (iStock)
Bringing back the spark
Elton suggested small ways to rebuild connection, including a 20-second hug or a six-second kiss.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Small acts of self-care, such as applying lotion or following a skincare routine, can also help people "feel more connected with themselves," she said.
DeSeta cautioned, however, that flirting may not always be welcomed by a partner, depending on timing and mood.
Pay attention to body language indicating your partner will be accepting of flirtatious advances. (iStock)

"I’ve heard from my couples, ‘They were trying to flirt with me when I was unloading the dishwasher,’" she noted as an example. "There’s a time and place for flirting, and you have to be in the right headspace."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Maybe when someone's in a stressed mood, they're really focused on work, or they're just doing a task that does not make them feel sexy — this is not the right time."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Positive signals from a partner, such as leaning in, making eye contact and smiling, can indicate that flirting is welcome.
Still, partners should communicate about when flirting feels appropriate, DeSeta added.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Your daily coffee habit could be taking a toll on your bones, new study suggests
summary: A Flinders University study links high coffee consumption to lower bone density in postmenopausal women, while tea's catechins may promote bone health.
story: Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, speaks about a new study linking hormone replacement therapy to lower dementia risk.
If you’re a woman who regularly reaches for coffee throughout the day, you may want to think twice about that next cup — or consider switching to tea.

Researchers at Flinders University reported in a study published in the journal Nutrients that high coffee consumption may be associated with lower bone mineral density (BMD) in older, postmenopausal women.

The scientists analyzed coffee and tea consumption among 9,704 women age 65 and older over a 10-year period. During that time, they also measured participants’ BMD at the femoral neck and hip, areas where osteoporosis-related fractures commonly occur.
The researchers found that drinking tea was associated with higher total hip BMD, while drinking more than five cups of coffee per day was associated with lower BMD.
COFFEE MAY HAVE POWERFUL EFFECT ON LIVER HEALTH, MAJOR STUDY SUGGESTS
Drinking more than five cups of coffee per day was associated with lower bone mineral density in older women, according to the study. (iStock)
Moderate coffee consumption — about two to three cups a day — was not associated with negative effects on bone health.

The study also identified differences based on other health and lifestyle factors. Coffee consumption was associated with lower femoral neck BMD among women with higher alcohol intake, while the positive association between tea and bone density was more pronounced among women with obesity.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The researchers wrote that osteoporosis, which is characterized by low BMD, "is a major global public health concern affecting individuals across all ages, genders and ethnicities."
About one in three women and one in five men age 50 and older worldwide experience osteoporosis-related fractures, according to the study.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Women face a particularly high risk because they generally have lower bone mass and experience accelerated bone loss after menopause.

In the U.S., the number of adults age 50 and older with low BMD in the hip or spine is projected to increase by 17.2 million by 2030, adding to the healthcare costs and long-term disability associated with osteoporosis-related fractures, the researchers noted.
Coffee lovers may not need to give up their daily brew, researchers said, but consuming more than five cups per day could be linked to lower bone density. (iStock)

The scientists wrote that they studied the relationship between coffee and tea and bone health because dietary factors play a "crucial role in the prevention of noncommunicable disease and may influence bone health," and these are two of the most widely consumed beverages globally.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Study co-author Ryan Liu told ScienceDaily "compounds called catechins, abundant in tea, may promote bone formation and slow bone breakdown."

"Coffee’s caffeine content, by contrast, has been shown in laboratory studies to interfere with calcium absorption and bone metabolism, though these effects are small and can be offset by adding milk," Liu said.
Older women who drank tea had higher bone density in the hip than those who did not, according to a study. (iStock)

"Our results don't mean you need to give up coffee or start drinking tea by the gallon," Liu added. "But they do suggest that moderate tea consumption could be one simple way to support bone health and that very high coffee intake might not be ideal, especially for women who drink alcohol."

"This study offers an interesting look at how everyday beverages might relate to bone health, but the findings should be interpreted with caution," Lisa Young, registered dietitian and adjunct professor of nutrition at New York University, told Fox News Digital.
"Because it followed women over time without assigning them to drink coffee or tea, it can only show associations, not prove that coffee weakens bones or that tea strengthens them."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study had limitations, including differences in participants’ lifestyles, its focus on bone density rather than fractures and relatively small effects seen mainly in older women, Young noted.
Symptoms of osteoporosis and early bone loss include back pain, loss of height over time and stooped posture, according to the Mayo Clinic.
"The bottom line for the public is reassuring: Moderate coffee intake appears fine, and there is no need to switch drinks for the sake of your bones," Young said.
"The most proven ways to protect bone health remain getting enough calcium and vitamin D, staying physically active and avoiding smoking and excess alcohol," she added.
"With that said, I do make a case for moderate amounts of coffee for good health. Too much of anything is never a good thing."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: The marriage warning sign that may be worse than fighting — and 4 ways to turn things around
summary: From flirting and dating to spending quality time without phones, experts share how small daily gestures can reverse quiet quitting in a marriage.
story: James Sexton explains how emotional withdrawal develops between couples, and why renewed attention, affection and mindfulness can reveal whether both partners remain invested.
Much like the workplace term that means doing the bare minimum, "quiet quitting" could also happen in marriage, sometimes gradually.

The informal term, which is not a clinical diagnosis, refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship, according to experts.
New York City divorce lawyer James Sexton described what "quiet quitting" can look like at home and at work.
"I'm not going to go through the dramatic gesture of ending this thing," Sexton said. "I'm just going to stop. I'm going to stop paying attention. I'm going to stop participating."
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

Silently pulling away from the relationship may seem to be easier than going through the "trauma" of divorce, Sexton told Fox News Digital, and the person avoids looking like the "bad guy" for ending the relationship.
"Very often, you actually receive more sympathy because you're perceived as the victim of the breakup as opposed to the perpetrator," he added.
"When people are fighting, it kind of means there’s still skin in the game," the divorce attorney said. (iStock)
A lack of effort in a relationship can be a bigger warning sign than frequent conflict, according to Sexton.
"When people are fighting, it kind of means there’s still skin in the game," he said. "The opposite of love is not hate … it’s indifference."
NEARLY 1 IN 3 MARRIED AMERICANS AREN'T HAVING SEX — EXPERT REVEALS HOW TO BRING BACK THE SPARK
Dr. Mindy DeSeta, a clinical sexologist and licensed mental health counselor in Miami, said some couples seek help after about 30 years of marriage, when the demands of family life have eased.

"The kids are gone, or they're hitting that retirement age, so they don't have the life distractions, and they're realizing, ‘Wow. I actually quiet quit my relationship when my kids were toddlers,’" she told Fox News Digital.
Some couples realize they've been out of their marriage since their children were young, an expert said. (iStock)
DeSeta identified four relationship principles, including the following:
Learning how to discuss physical and sexual intimacy
Focusing on teamwork
Staying autonomous
"Learning and earning" your partner through constant dating
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Couples experiencing quiet quitting may continue to function well as a team, managing the household and other responsibilities while becoming emotionally disconnected.
DeSeta said this disconnection can develop gradually as spouses begin living increasingly separate lives.
"Quiet quitting" your relationship can show up in subtle signs like taking interests in different things or going to bed at separate times. (iStock)

"When you stop spending the evenings together … you each are kind of doing your own thing. Your shows are different. You're going to bed at different times. … You may have different friend groups. You're working out at different times," she said.
4 tips to turn it around
Both experts shared tips for addressing emotional disconnection between romantic partners.
Reconnection often requires small, active steps that restart the momentum, rather than making grand gestures, Sexton suggested.
"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you. They're loaned."
The divorce lawyer encouraged revisiting the simple acts and gestures that both partners enjoyed early in the relationship.
His suggestions included sending sweet "good morning" texts, writing a note complimenting a partner or sharing a song that sparked a romantic memory.

"It costs nothing, takes 30 seconds to do it," he said. "What does it cost to write an email with a list of 10 things I like about you? These are not only things we welcome receiving under any circumstances, but they're actually reminders."
Oftentimes, quiet quitting looks like zoning out during moments of quality time, DeSeta said.
If one partner scrolls on a phone while watching a movie together, the device can become "the third member of the relationship," signaling where that partner’s attention lies, the expert cautioned.
"When you're on your phone, you're just actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending this quality time with you,’" an expert said. (iStock)
"When you're on your phone, you're actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending quality time with you,'" she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In addition to paying attention during one-on-one activities, the act of asking personal questions — as simple as "how was your day?" — can also help to restore a connection, DeSeta said.
Instead of leading with a complaint about the relationship, Sexton suggested using a positive approach.
For example, instead of saying, "We never spend time with each other anymore," try calling back a positive memory and suggest recreating it.
Communicating positively is more likely to receive a positive response, experts advise. (iStock)

"Focusing on what we need to work on is harder than focusing on what it is that we really like about this person, what drew us to them to begin with," he said. "Chances are, they might feel far away from who they were at the beginning of the relationship.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"And maybe our job in a relationship is to try to remind each other of the 'you' and the 'me' before we became the 'we.'"
Making an active effort to flirt with a partner can boost your mood while signaling continued romantic interest, according to DeSeta.
"Let your partner know that you are there to earn them every day," she said, emphasizing the importance of continuing to learn about and pursue a partner throughout the relationship.
The relationship expert emphasized the importance of consistently "learning and earning" your partner. (iStock)

"Let them know in the most subtle ways every single day that you care about them, that you're thinking about them. And if you do that, you kind of break this cycle of the quiet quitting, and, eventually, it starts coming back to you."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Sexton reminded couples that their time together is limited, so illness or tragedy should not be the catalyst for renewed effort.

"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you. They're loaned," he said. "There’s a finite number of times that you're going to be with this person, see this person, tell this person that you love them."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Scientists discover new tick-borne virus after testing thousands of patients with mysterious illnesses
summary: The Asian longhorned tick nairovirus caused flu-like illness and thrombocytopenia in over 10% of tick-bitten patients studied in a China lab.
story: Dr. Sharon Nachman, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital in New York, shares what to know about the newly discovered Asian longhorned tick nairovirus.
Scientists in China have identified a previously unknown tick-borne virus that can cause flu-like illness, fatigue and gastrointestinal symptoms, according to a new study.

The newly discovered virus, the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), which is part of the orthonairovirus group, has also been found to cause thrombocytopenia (reduced blood platelet counts) and laboratory evidence of liver-cell injury or inflammation.

Since 2009, Chinese researchers have been tracking patients with unusual illnesses, including severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), according to Dr. Sharon Nachman, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital in New York.
NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE
"Thrombocytopenia is low platelet count, so those patients bled, and it had about a 30% mortality, which is quite high," she told Fox News Digital. "So, they kept following those patients."
Many of the cases were linked to Dabie bandavirus (DBV), a tick-borne hemorrhagic fever, but it was not the most common virus.

The newly discovered virus, the Asian longhorned tick nairovirus, which is part of the orthonairovirus group, has also been found to cause thrombocytopenia (reduced blood platelet counts) and laboratory evidence of liver-cell injury or inflammation. (Getty Images)
After extensive testing of blood samples and viral fragments, researchers identified the new virus, ALTNV, which is genetically distinct from DBV.
Researchers from the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing identified the virus in 10.4% of 3,163 patients who had been bitten by ticks.
HANTAVIRUS IN THE US: WHERE THE RARE, SOMETIMES DEADLY DISEASE HAS BEEN FOUND
Patients who had both ALTNV and DBV were more likely to have respiratory issues and kidney complications. Seven (18.4%) of these patients died during the course of the study.

"The cocirculation of ALTNV and DBV in the same areas, coupled with their shared tick vector, underscores the need for improved differential diagnosis between infections with these viruses in regions where SFTS is endemic," the authors concluded.
Because tick-borne viral symptoms can overlap with many infections, a doctor emphasized the importance of identifying the specific virus. (iStock)
The findings were published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The big picture is that ticks carry lots of viruses," Nachman said. "We're getting smarter at identifying those viruses. And when one blood sample is negative, it's important to say, 'Maybe there was a new virus there, and let's look for it.'"
Symptoms and treatment
Illness from ALTNV can initially resemble the flu, causing fever, muscle aches, fatigue and sometimes respiratory symptoms.

Although an ALTNV infection can cause low platelet counts, the study did not link the virus alone to severe bleeding or deaths. The fatal cases involved patients who were also infected with DBV, which causes severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome.
Illness from ALTNV can initially resemble the flu, causing fever, muscle aches, fatigue and sometimes respiratory symptoms. (iStock)
Because tick-borne viral symptoms can overlap with many infections, Nachman emphasized the importance of identifying the specific virus.
"Effective antivirals exist for flu, but not for many tick-borne viruses, including the newly identified one," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

For most patients, supportive care is given to help manage symptoms, "but it's also about being smart and not giving patients the wrong medication," Nachman noted. "And we certainly don't want to use antibiotics because those only work for bacteria, not for viruses."
Preventing tick bites
Nachman shared the best practices she recommends to families looking to avoid tick bites.
"Wear the right clothing, meaning long pants, tucking them into your socks, and use tick repellents on your skin if you're an adult or on your clothing if you're a young child," she advised.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
It’s also important to be on the lookout for ticks on the skin.

"The longer the tick is on your skin, the more it's engorged, the more it’s likely to pass an infection to you," Nachman said. "So, removing them after you've gone hiking or walking on the beach will be really important."
People who are bitten by ticks should remove them as soon as possible. (iStock)
While the Asian longhorn tick is not yet seen in the U.S., Nachman noted there are "lots and lots of other ticks, and those ticks carry other diseases."
"I don't want to say one tick is worse than another tick. It's rather all about the diseases they carry and who you are," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"So, if you're a healthy adult, and you get babesiosis, you often get better without any medications. But if you're an immune-compromised adult, you're going to be quite sick.
"It’s not really about the ticks. It’s about the patient. Who are you? What's your underlying illness if you have any? How old are you, and how healthy are you?"
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Common cholesterol drug linked to lower dementia risk when started early
summary: A massive study found that starting statins within a year of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis was linked to a 15% lower risk of dementia over a decade.
story: A geriatrician explains why starting statins soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may be linked to lower dementia risk, particularly vascular dementia, while stressing that a recent study does not prove causation.
Starting statin therapy shortly after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may not only protect the heart — it may also be linked to a lower dementia risk.

A large study presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich on Aug. 30 found that adults who began taking a statin within one year of their type 2 diabetes diagnosis had a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years compared to those who did not take the medication within five years.
Even for those who delayed starting a statin for one to five years, there was still a 10% lower relative risk, according to the findings, which were published in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS
A statin is a prescription medication that lowers "bad" LDL cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Researchers conducted the study by tracking health data from 132,585 patients in Denmark who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2006 and 2019 and had no prior history of statin use or dementia.
A statin is a prescription medication that lowers "bad" LDL cholesterol and helps reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. (iStock)
During a median follow-up of 7.1 years, the team analyzed how the timing of statin treatment impacted overall dementia rates.

Dr. Liron Sinvani, a geriatrician and director for research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging in New York, said this was a "well-designed, large-scale observational study that adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that statins may help protect brain health."
GAME-CHANGING CHOLESTEROL PILL WINS FDA APPROVAL AFTER CUTTING LDL NEARLY 60%
She noted that while a 15% reduction is a modest improvement, it remains "very significant."
People with type 2 diabetes have an increased risk of cognitive decline and heart disease, consistent with previous research.

Starting a statin within one year of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis was associated with a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years, while delaying treatment reduced the benefit to 10%. (iStock)
Although guidelines generally recommend statins for many adults ages 40 to 75 with diabetes, statin treatment is not always started soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis.

The study also examined whether the timing of treatment was linked to dementia risk. People who started statins within a year of their diagnosis had a lower risk than those who did not begin treatment.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach," Sinvani said, supporting earlier consideration of statin therapy in routine diabetes care.
The expert said she found the results "especially compelling" because the benefit was driven by a lower risk of vascular dementia rather than Alzheimer's disease.
"The message here is that maybe waiting is actually not the right approach."

"And that makes biological sense, because we know statins lower cholesterol, reduces inflammation and protects blood vessels," she added, pointing out that these same mechanisms prevent vascular damage to the brain.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Statin therapy should be viewed as one piece of a broader health strategy alongside exercising regularly, adhering to a healthy diet and staying socially connected, according to the expert.
Because this was an observational study rather than a randomized controlled trial, the findings show a strong association but do not prove a direct causal link. (iStock)
Almost half of dementia cases may be preventable or delayable by addressing modifiable risk factors, according to the Lancet Commission.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The study did have limitations. Because it was observational rather than a randomized clinical trial, the researchers could not definitively state that statins directly prevent dementia.
As Sinvani cautioned, "This is not proof that statins prevent dementia, but I think it's an important step in this literature."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor encouraged people with type 2 diabetes who are not taking a statin to ask their doctor whether the medication is appropriate for them."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Marijuana users may face hidden driving danger that standard tests can miss
summary: Cannabis edible users registered THC levels nearly 10 times lower than smokers despite similar driving impairment, exposing a potential road safety gap.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail a new study linking marijuana use to heart disease and discuss data suggesting diet and exercise could help cancer patients.
A new study warns that driving after eating cannabis edibles can significantly impair road performance and reaction times, even if blood tests show THC levels far below the legal limit.
The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, highlight a potential challenge for impaired-driving enforcement in Canada and some U.S. jurisdictions.

Most previous cannabis-driving studies have involved smoked or inhaled marijuana, which more rapidly spikes levels of THC (tetrahydrocannabinol, the main psychoactive compound in cannabis) in the bloodstream.
AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING
Edibles are absorbed more slowly and can produce driving impairment even when blood THC concentrations remain relatively low.

Researchers found that drivers who consumed higher doses of edible THC struggled with lane control, had slower reaction times and experienced greater speed fluctuations. Yet, their blood tests stayed below the standard legal cutoff used to prove impairment at roadside traffic stops.
Researchers measured how well drivers stayed in their lane, how quickly they reacted to road events and how consistently they maintained their speed. (iStock)
To assess how oral cannabis impacts driving, researchers at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto conducted a trial with 40 healthy adult volunteers who regularly use cannabis.
Each participant attended four separate sessions in which they consumed soft-chew gummies containing either 0, 2, 10 or 20 milligrams of THC.
CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS

The researchers then tested the drivers using a driving simulator at two, five and 24 hours after consumption, tracking how well drivers stayed in their lane, how quickly they reacted to road events and how consistently they maintained their speed.
Blood samples and self-reported ratings of intoxication were also collected.
Participants recognized their own limitations, reporting a lower willingness to drive and reduced confidence in their driving skills after taking the gummies. (iStock)

The results showed driving impairment at two and five hours after consuming 10- and 20-milligram gummies. Compared with placebo, participants who consumed those doses had greater variability in lane position, while the 20-milligram dose was also linked to slower reaction times and less consistent speed control.
Participants also recognized their own limitations, reporting a lower willingness to drive and reduced confidence in their driving skills after taking the gummies.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The highest blood THC concentrations averaged 1.6 nanograms per milliliter after the 10-milligram dose and 3.4 nanograms per milliliter after the 20-milligram dose. Those levels were below the commonly used 5-ng/mL threshold, although THC limits vary by jurisdiction and some individual samples exceeded 5 ng/mL.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

By comparison, participants in the team’s previous smoked-cannabis study showed similar levels of impairment while reaching an average peak blood THC concentration of 30.3 nanograms per milliliter, nearly 10 times higher than the 20-milligram edible group.

The study did have some limitations. Tests were conducted on virtual simulators rather than actual roads, meaning drivers faced no real physical risk during the experiments. It also focused on regular cannabis users, so it is unclear how occasional users might react to similar doses.

When the research team previously tested smoked marijuana, drivers with similar impairment levels registered blood THC concentrations averaging 30.3 nanograms per milliliter, nearly 10 times higher. (iStock)

Additionally, minimal residual effects were detected after 24 hours. While maximum speed remained slightly higher among participants on the 10-milligram and 20-milligram doses, subjective feelings of intoxication had completely faded.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
In an accompanying commentary, Dr. José Ignacio Nazif-Munoz of the Université de Sherbrooke noted that these biological differences pose a challenge for law enforcement.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Because edibles are absorbed slowly through the digestive system, standard blood tests may fail to identify unsafe drivers, leaving policymakers searching for more reliable roadside tools.
"The delayed absorption and prolonged duration of effects of edible cannabis distinguish it from smoked or inhaled cannabis, complicating the interpretation of biological measures," he wrote.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Deadly mosquito-borne virus claims first life in major US city as cases spread
summary: Chicago's first West Nile virus death of 2026 follows the city's rainiest summer in years, as CDPH sprays insecticide across 15 community areas.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, discusses the spread, symptoms and management of West Nile virus.
A Chicago resident has died from West Nile virus, marking the city’s first death linked to the mosquito-borne illness this year, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health.
Several other cases have been reported throughout Illinois.

The virus is most commonly spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito, although the disease cycle also includes infected birds. When mosquitoes feed on infected birds, they can pick up the virus and transmit it to humans.
2 AIRPORT WORKERS ARE DEAD AFTER MALARIA CASES SHOCK OFFICIALS AT MAJOR TRAVEL HUB
"2026 has seen the rainiest summer in Chicago in years, giving mosquitoes ample opportunities to breed," CDPH Commissioner Garth Walker said in a statement.
"The best way to protect yourself from West Nile virus is to avoid mosquito bites and take measures to stop them from breeding around your home."
A Chicago resident has died from West Nile virus, marking the city’s first death linked to the mosquito-borne illness this year, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. (iStock)

In an attempt to prevent infections, the CDPH has sprayed insecticide in the following community areas: Beverly, Burnside, Chatham, East Garfield Park, the Lower West Side, Morgan Park, the Near West Side, North Lawndale, O'Hare, Pullman, Roseland, South Deering, Washington Heights, West Lawn and West Pullman.
Symptoms and treatment
For most people, West Nile produces mild symptoms — such as fever, aches and rashes — or none at all, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
VACATION HOT SPOT FACES NEW CDC TRAVEL WARNING AS OUTBREAK CASES CONTINUE CLIMBING
In rare serious cases, the virus invades the nervous system, causing meningitis, encephalitis (swelling of the brain), paralysis or death.
People over 50 or those with compromised immune systems are at highest risk, experts caution.
West Nile virus is most commonly spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito, although the disease cycle also includes infected birds.  (iStock)

"Of those who do have symptoms, about 20%, maybe 25%, will have the flu-like symptoms — fever, headache, body aches — and it’s very hard to distinguish between that and flu," Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
There are also rare, severe neuroinvasive cases, when the virus infects the brain.
"When there's inflammation that leads to meningitis or encephalitis, that's very bad," warned Evans, who is also the CEO and chief medical officer for Wellness Equity Alliance.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"So if there's ever any severe headaches, stiff neck, disorientation, vision loss, feeling like you're just really confused, and if you're over the age of 65, or have immunocompromising conditions like severe diabetes or cancers, that's when you're going to want to seek emergency management as quickly as possible."
While there are no vaccines or specific treatments for West Nile virus, there are supportive treatments.
For most people, West Nile produces mild symptoms — such as fever, aches and rashes — or none at all, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (iStock)
"For the flu-like symptoms, generally speaking, if you're not over the age of 65 and you're not immunocompromised, you don't have to go to the emergency room," Evans advised.
"But if you are over the age of 65 and/or have those immunocompromising conditions, and you're starting to experience confusion, headache, stiff neck … ER immediately, [call] 911."
Prevention tips
Avoiding mosquito bites is the first line of defense, according to Evans.
"In areas where there are a lot of mosquitoes, DEET is going to be key," he said, recommending repellents that are at least 30% DEET for adults.
In high-burden mosquito areas, he also recommends avoiding the outdoors during sundown.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Health officials also recommend wearing loose, long-sleeved clothing; applying insect repellent (especially at dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most active); and ensuring that window screens are secure.
Around homes, eliminating standing water (like that found in buckets, tires and gutters) can help keep mosquitoes from breeding.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

There have been 407 reported human cases of West Nile virus in the U.S. this year, including 285 severe neuroinvasive cases and 23 deaths, according to the latest preliminary CDC data, current as of Sept. 1.
Most West Nile cases are reported in August and September.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Popular diet slashes liver fat by 67% while reversing prediabetes in some people
summary: A keto diet reduced liver fat by roughly 67% and reversed prediabetes in half of participants, but the study's small sample size is a caveat.
story: Registered dietitian Ilana Muhlstein discusses research comparing ketogenic, Mediterranean and plant-forward eating patterns, including their effects on hepatic fat, glucose control and metabolic health.
The keto diet may have surprising benefits for liver health, a new study suggests.
The research, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, studied 42 adults who had obesity, prediabetes and excess liver fat.
In a randomized clinical trial, the participants were assigned to three weight-loss diets – a low-carb ketogenic diet, a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat, mostly plant-based diet.
SECRET TO WEIGHT LOSS MAY BE HIDING IN YOUR GUT, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

The keto diet’s calories consisted of about 4% carbohydrates and 73% fat, according to the study. The Mediterranean diet provided about 50% of calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat, while the low-fat diet provided about 70% of calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.
In all three groups, muscle insulin sensitivity improved by about 50%, helping the muscles take up blood sugar more efficiently.
Liver fat decreased by roughly 67% in those following the keto diet, compared to about 45% with the other diets. (iStock)
Liver insulin sensitivity improved two to three times as much in the keto group as in the other diet groups.

Liver fat decreased by roughly 67% among people following the keto diet, compared with about 45% among those on the other diets. The reduction was linked to a decrease in the liver’s production of new fat.

Glucose and insulin measures also generally improved more in the keto group. About 50% of participants in that group no longer met the criteria for prediabetes by the end of the trial, compared with 29% of those following the Mediterranean diet and 7% of those on the low-fat diet.
ONE COMMON TYPE OF FAT MAY INCREASE DIABETES RISK, WHILE ANOTHER HELPS FIGHT IT
The study’s short duration and small sample size — about 14 people in each diet group — limit how broadly the findings can be applied to the general population, the researchers said.

The researchers concluded that, among people with obesity, prediabetes and excess liver fat, the composition of a weight-loss diet may influence certain metabolic outcomes beyond the effects of weight loss alone. The keto diet produced the greatest improvements in liver fat and liver insulin sensitivity in this small trial.
People on the keto diet saw two to three times greater improvements in how well their liver responded to insulin. (iStock)
Registered dietitian nutritionist Ilana Muhlstein reflected on the study findings.
"I love more and more validation and recognition that calories are not equal," the California-based expert told Fox News Digital.

Muhlstein said people often reduce weight loss to "just a calorie deficit," but this study showed that differences in macronutrients were associated with different changes in health markers despite similar weight loss.
POPULAR DIET TREND COULD BOOST MENTAL HEALTH AMONG OLDER ADULTS, STUDY FINDS

Although weight loss occurred across all three groups, Muhlstein said the participants experienced different internal metabolic changes. The keto group showed a greater reduction in the liver’s production of new fat, along with metabolic changes consistent with greater fat burning.
Anyone with a fatty liver should consider transitioning to a lower carbohydrate diet, a nutritionist advised. (iStock)
Muhlstein explained that excess calories and metabolic dysfunction can cause fat to accumulate in the liver, even in people who do not drink alcohol.
She recommends that anyone with a fatty liver should consider transitioning to a lower carbohydrate diet.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Muhlstein said reducing carbohydrate intake may encourage the body to use more stored fat for energy.
The findings were notable because the keto group did not experience higher cholesterol or blood-fat measurements during the short study, the expert noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"This is a really interesting study for someone who has prediabetes, someone who had blood sugar irregularity, but maybe still something to be cautious of if someone has heart disease in the family or is at high risk of heart disease," she added.
After achieving significant weight loss, the nutritionist recommends transitioning to something closer to the Mediterranean diet for "long-term overall health." (iStock)

Overall, Muhlstein said the findings suggest keto may be worth discussing as a short-term option for some people with obesity or prediabetes, particularly because the study found greater reductions in liver fat and higher rates of prediabetes remission — even though weight loss was similar across the three groups.

"Keto is not something I recommend for anyone long-term because of the high saturated fat, and usually it translates into a lower-fiber diet, which is not good for heart health," Muhlstein said.

title: Women who start common hormone therapy in their 50s may have 23% lower dementia risk
summary: Hormone replacement therapy started between ages 46 and 56 was tied to lower Alzheimer's and dementia risk, a major new UK Biobank study suggests.
story: Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, speaks about a new study linking hormone replacement therapy to lower dementia risk.
Women who start hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at a certain age may have a lower dementia risk, a new study suggests.
The study, published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, analyzed UK Biobank data of 183,450 postmenopausal women averaging 60 years of age.
The U.K. researchers determined that HRT use was associated with about a 10% lower risk of all-cause dementia and a 16% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease over a 13-year follow-up period.
'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS
The association was strongest among women who started the therapy between the ages of 46 and 56. It was also high among those who had undergone surgical menopause.
Starting HRT after age 56 was not associated with reduced dementia risk.
Women who start hormone replacement therapy at a certain age may have a lower dementia risk, a new study suggests. (iStock)

Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, noted that this was an observational study that can’t show cause and effect.
"So, it kind of stays where the data has been for a while — that in certain patients, we have no evidence that it really makes a difference," she told Fox News Digital.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH

"And, for some patients, such as [those] who go through menopause a little bit younger, whether that's surgically or naturally, or if they have that APOE ε4 genotype that predisposes them to dementia, there may be some benefit."
Study limitations
The researchers also stated that since this was an observational study, it could not establish that HRT prevents dementia but only showed an association.
The study also did not assess any safety outcomes or adverse events related to HRT.
Women who use HRT may differ from non-users in other ways that affect dementia risk, such as their overall health, lifestyle or access to healthcare, the researchers noted.
There is some data linking menopausal symptoms, such as hot flashes and night sweats, with vascular changes in the brain, a doctor noted. (iStock)
Although researchers adjusted for many of these factors, some unmeasured differences could still factor into the lower dementia risk seen among HRT users.
The study also did not have detailed information on the types of hormone therapy, the way they were administered or the specific dosages women took.
"If you're having symptoms, if you feel not yourself, come in, talk to your doctor, have that conversation."
Most of the people in the study were of European ancestry and tended to be better off financially, so the findings may not apply equally to people from other populations.
This study alone likely doesn't warrant seeking out HRT just for dementia prevention, Fiffick said.
"However, if you're having symptoms, if you feel not yourself, come in, talk to your doctor, have that conversation," she advised.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
There is some data linking menopausal symptoms, such as hot flashes and night sweats, with vascular changes in the brain, the doctor noted.
"So, we are very hopeful to see that treating those symptoms may prevent the vascular changes that lead to vascular dementia, but we just don't have that data right now," she said.
"So, it's worth the conversation, it's worth bringing up, but I wouldn't go out of your way for just this purpose."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
HRT does carry some known risks and side effects, Fiffick noted.
For oral versions of estrogen, there may be an increased risk of blood clots. That risk does not appear to exist for transdermal options, such as patches, gels and creams.
As this was an observational study, it could not establish that HRT prevents dementia but only showed an association. (iStock)
Other types of HRT may impact breast activity, overall inflammation, cardiovascular markers and cardiometabolic markers, according to the doctor.
"So, it's not one size fits all, and it's really worth an extensive conversation."
Looking ahead

The U.K. researchers plan to conduct randomized controlled trials to confirm that HRT reduces dementia risk. Future studies will include factors such as estrogen-only versus combined therapy, dosage amounts, administration route, treatment duration, age at the start of therapy, menopause type and potentially APOE genotype.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I think the more we have studies like this, the more we're going to propel forward the randomized controlled trials to really give women the data they deserve," Fiffick concluded.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Women deserve to have information to use to make decisions about their bodies. So I'm excited to see the trends heading in that direction."

title: New weight-loss compound melts fat without curbing appetite — and preserves muscle
summary: University of California, Berkeley scientists found TOFA boosted energy expenditure in obese mice without the lean muscle loss tied to semaglutide.
story: Dr. Leslie Pristas, a bariatric surgeon and owner of Best Life Bariatrics and Medical Weight Loss in Ohio, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential of an experimental obesity therapy.
A team of researchers led by scientists at the University of California, Berkeley, has identified a decades-old oral compound that produced substantial weight loss in obese mice.
Rather than suppressing appetite, the compound appears to boost energy expenditure, according to a study published in Science Advances.
The molecule, known as TOFA, reduced the mice’s body weight by an average of 18% without changing how much they ate or causing a statistically significant loss of lean mass.
NEW OBESITY TREATMENT MAY HELP PRESERVE MUSCLE DURING WEIGHT LOSS

While popular injectable weight-loss medications such as semaglutide can produce substantial weight loss partly by reducing food intake, some patients experience gastrointestinal side effects and loss of lean mass.
Studies have also found that people often regain a significant amount of weight after stopping treatment.
Researchers found that an oral compound called TOFA produced substantial weight loss in obese mice by boosting energy expenditure rather than suppressing appetite like GLP-1s. (iStock)
Preserving muscle during weight loss remains one of the greatest clinical hurdles in obesity medicine, according to experts.

"Muscle mass is really important for our function during the day. It helps fight the effects of aging," Dr. Leslie Pristas, a bariatric surgeon and owner of Best Life Bariatrics and Medical Weight Loss in Northeast Ohio, told Fox News Digital.
"Building muscle is really hard. It takes a really long time. So if we can avoid having muscle loss while we're having weight loss, that's going to be so much better."
THIS COULD BE WHY YOUR WEIGHT-LOSS MEDICATION ISN’T DELIVERING RESULTS

Instead of primarily targeting appetite, TOFA acts inside cells, according to the researchers. It blocks enzymes involved in the production of lipids, including fats such as triglycerides, while also activating cellular receptors that turn on genes involved in fat burning and energy production.
Treated mice burned up to 18% more energy under room-temperature and mildly warm conditions, without becoming less active or developing a dangerous increase in body temperature.
Preserving muscle during weight loss is critical for long-term health, as a bariatric surgeon noted that muscle protects daily physical function and helps combat aging. (iStock)

When the researchers combined TOFA with existing obesity drugs such as semaglutide or tirzepatide, the combination treatments produced greater reductions in body weight and improvements in blood sugar, insulin and triglyceride levels than either drug alone.
Mice treated with TOFA maintained body weights close to control levels after treatment ended, while mice previously given semaglutide began rapidly regaining weight.
PATIENTS TAKING WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS OFTEN MAKE 5 CRITICAL MISTAKES, DOCTOR WARNS
Pristas urged caution against assuming that any single medication could permanently prevent post-treatment weight gain.
"Obesity is super complex," she said. "There's not just one mechanism by which everyone gains weight or even a single person gains weight. There are a lot of overlapping factors."
"If we can avoid having muscle loss while we're having weight loss, that's going to be so much better."

"Once we have extra weight on our body, that kind of becomes where our body thinks we're supposed to be. That becomes our body's weight set point," she noted, adding that if someone stops a medication abruptly, the body may then work to return to its previous weight.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The compound also showed promise in mouse models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a form of fatty liver disease. Mice given TOFA had less liver fat, inflammation and fibrosis (scarring).
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

TOFA achieved these liver benefits without increasing triglyceride levels in the blood, the researchers noted. Some similar metabolic drugs have caused triglycerides to rise, creating potential cardiovascular and other health concerns that have complicated their development.
Study limitations
The authors emphasized that all the animal experiments involved male mice. Future studies will need to determine whether TOFA produces similar results in female animals.

The drug has not yet been tested in people, so researchers still don't know what dose would be appropriate, whether it is safe to use over long periods, or whether it could cause subtle toxicities or other safety problems.
Patients concerned about their weight-loss journey should speak to a professional before making any medication changes. (iStock)
Pristas emphasized that early mouse data must be weighed carefully against potential hidden side effects in humans.
"If it sounds too good to be true, it's probably too good to be true," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"When you're talking about manipulating our bodies' manufacturing or processing of lipids, it's complex. And so there can be downstream effects that we don't want. That's where we can't get too excited."
However, the expert said the treatment could eventually benefit people, either on its own or in combination with another therapy.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study authors disclosed that several researchers are co-founders, officers or equity holders in ReRx Therapeutics, a company with an agreement giving it the option to develop UC Berkeley’s TOFA-related discovery.
