Anyone who violates the order could face criminal charges under Italian law.
Fox News Digital reached out to Rome police for additional information.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: US-backed effort to disarm Iraq’s Iran-linked militias hits setback, experts say
summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi vowed to restrict weapons to state control, but militias like Asaib Ahl al-Haq show no credible disarmament evidence.
story: President Donald Trump says Iraq is ready to stand on its own without U.S. troops, while Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says armed groups outside state control will have "no justification" after the coalition mission ends.
The Trump administration’s push to compel the new Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to dismantle pro-Iran terrorist militias is moving forward — even with some setbacks.

As Mideast experts are taking a wait-and-see approach tinged with mild optimism, a senior Iraqi official announced in late August that Baghdad will not treat Sept. 30 as a deadline to disarm the pro-Iran groups known as the Popular Mobilization Units (PMU), also called the Popular Mobilization Forces.

The Iraqi government is seeking to exercise control over the rogue state-affiliated militias with a strategy to integrate them into the state apparatus. The radical Iraqi Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, who leads Saraya al-Salam armed group, said in May that he favored integration. Some of the more hardline pro-Iranian regime militias, like Kataeb Hezbollah and Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, declared that they will not disarm or integrate into the state.

The official, Qasim al-Araji, security advisor to the prime minister, told Al Iraqiya on Aug. 23, "Sept. 30 is the date for the international coalition to depart, not the deadline to hand over weapons." The international coalition is the U.S.-led force that defeated the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria during President Trump’s first term. It is unclear why Iraq’s government is walking back the disarmament deadline for the PMU.
IRAN'S WAR ON AMERICANS BEGAN DECADES AGO. THESE FAMILIES STILL CARRY THE SCARS
President Donald Trump gestures toward Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi as they meet in the Oval Office at the White House, July 14, 2026. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)
A spokesman for the Iraqi embassy declined to comment on the mixed messaging from Iraq’s government and on the timetable for dissolving or integrating the PMU.

Just days before al-Araji’s announcement, a representative of the Iraqi government sent Fox News Digital a statement: "Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi: All political forces fully agree on moving forward with restricting weapons to state control, and work is underway on mechanisms for surrendering weapons and bringing this issue to a complete end."

Al-Zaidi told the Baghdad Dialogue Conference at the same time that "all political forces agree on moving forward to ensure that all arms remain under state authority and on developing mechanisms for the handover of weapons. There are no intentions or prospects of any military confrontation, and we will not allow Iraq’s enemies to exploit any opportunity. The presence of weapons outside state authority creates an environment that discourages investment, which is unacceptable because it does not serve the interests of Iraqis."

Members of the Islamic Movement of Iraq — a faction of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) paramilitaries — gather during a rally to mark annual Quds (Jerusalem) Day commemorations in Baghdad on April 5, 2024. (Murtaj Lateef/AFP via Getty Images)

In May, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Ali Maarij Al-Bahadly, Iraq’s deputy minister of oil, because he, according to the designation, "abuses his position to facilitate the diversion of oil to be sold for the benefit of the Iranian regime and its proxy militias in Iraq." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time, "Like a rogue gang, the Iranian regime is pillaging resources that rightfully belong to the Iraqi people," adding "Treasury will not stand idly by as Iran's military exploits Iraqi oil to fund terrorism against the United States and our partners."

In late August, the UAE's The National paper reported that "Iraq's anti-corruption body announced that deputy oil minister, Al-Bahadly, was sentenced to seven years in prison and fined millions of dollars for corruption.

Reacting to reports that Iran approved passage of Iraqi oil tankers via the Strait of Hormuz, Alberto Fernandez, former U.S. ambassador and Mideast analyst, claimed that "the profit from that Iraqi oil goes, in part, to pay for Iran’s own Iraqi militias/death squads on the Iraqi government’s payroll."
An Iraqi government spokesman dismissed Fernandez's comments, telling Fox News Digital, "That is not accurate."
TRUMP’S COUNTERTERRORISM STRATEGY SCORES BIG WINS AGAINST GLOBAL TERROR THREATS
Demonstrators in Basra, Iraq, on Feb. 28, 2026, protest U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran. (Haidar Mohammed Ali/Anadolu via Getty Images)

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "Iraq has embarked on a new direction under the leadership of Prime Minister Al-Zaidi in full partnership with the United States. As President Trump made clear when he hosted Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s historic July 14 visit, the United States strongly supports his vision to ensure a brighter future for all Iraqis free from terrorism, to prevent attacks in and from Iraqi territory, and to deliver a strong and mutually beneficial U.S.-Iraq partnership."

Entifadh Qanbar, a former spokesman for the deputy prime minister of Iraq during the George W. Bush administration, told Fox News Digital: "We were all hoping that Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi would take decisive action against the militias, especially after his visit to the White House and the widespread praise he received from President Trump. I was always skeptical, very skeptical, but I believed he deserved a chance."

Qanbar added, "Initially, some militias such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali (sanctioned by the U.S.) merely issued statements claiming they would hand over their weapons. There has been no credible evidence that they have actually disarmed."
IRAN’S GUTTED RANKS LEAVE LOYALISTS FILLING CRITICAL POSTS — WITH ONE GLARING PROBLEM
Esmail Qaani, commander of the IRGC Quds Force, participates in a religious ceremony in Tehran on June 13. (Anonymous/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

Qanbar claimed that "any remaining hope was further diminished after IRGC [Islamic Republic Guard Corps] Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani visited Baghdad. According to multiple reports, he instructed militia leaders to slow down any discussion of disarmament, reject the September 30 deadline, and maintain their weapons as part of Iran’s broader regional deterrence strategy."

When asked about Iraqi state efforts to dismantle the PMU, Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior non-resident fellow at the New Lines Institute in Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital, "The Iraqi government is trying. It genuinely carried out some moves. Unfortunately, because the militias are extremely willing to use force against their own people, including against security forces, the government finds itself in a position of backing down in the face of these militias."

She noted, "The militias have penetrated most state institutions… and you see repeated situations of the state backing down." Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iran-backed group designated by the U.S. as a terrorist organization, kidnapped Tsurkov in 2023 and held her hostage for nearly two years. The Trump administration secured her release in 2025.
The power of the PMU was demonstrated in a recent setback for the Iraqi government.
Masked Iran-backed Shi'ite fighters hold their weapons in Iraq's Al Hadidiya, south of Tikrit, en route to the Islamic State-controlled al-Alam town, on March 6, 2015. (Reuters/Thaier Al-Sudani)

Both Qanbar and Tsurkov cited the case of the Iraqi Counter Terrorism Service (CTS), which arrested Abbas al-Yaqubi, the head of intelligence for the Popular Mobilization Forces’ Baghdad Belt Operations Command.

A few days after al-Yaqubi’s arrest, he was transferred to the PMU intelligence branch. Qanbar said: "Al-Yaqubi has long been involved in violence against Iraqi activists, and many viewed his arrest as an important signal that the government was finally willing to confront powerful militia figures. What seemed like a significant step forward turned into a major setback."

title: Anti-migrant AfD seeks to break Germany’s political ‘firewall’ in historic state election
summary: Young voters are fueling Germany's AfD surge in Saxony-Anhalt, where lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund has amassed over 700,000 TikTok followers.
story: Nile Gardiner weighs in after European voters appeared to reject far-left progressive policies, leading to significant conservative gains across the continent.

A political earthquake is brewing in Germany's east as working-class and young voters appear set to deliver an unprecedented victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Sunday’s state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.

The AfD, which was famously backed by Elon Musk in last year’s national election, has been criticized for being pro-Russia and was accused of being a "right-wing extremist endeavor" by Germany’s domestic intelligence office, has the chance to become the first party outside the mainstream center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) or center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), to win an outright majority in a German state parliament, or Landtag, since World War II.

"The reason Saxony-Anhalt matters," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, who holds a doctorate in political science from Berlin's Humboldt University, told Fox News Digital, "is that the AfD is no longer just knocking on the door of power. It may be close to kicking it open."
TENS OF THOUSANDS OF FAR-LEFT PROTESTERS CLASH WITH POLICE IN ANTI-CONSERVATIVE PARTY RIOTS

Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic candidate with broad appeal in the state, has helped propel the AfD to 43% in state polls, far ahead of other parties. The AfD could possibly win with a majority in the state parliament and form a state government, which would be a first for the party. Saxony-Anhalt will hold elections on Sept. 6. (Getty Images)

Other minor parties have led governing coalitions in German states, but no party outside the SPD or the CDU and the CSU has ever held a single-party governing majority in Germany since the Federal Republic was re-established in 1949.

Janek Treiber, a political science researcher at Dresden University of Technology, told Fox News Digital that if the AfD does win outright in Saxony-Anhalt, their policy influence would be limited due to the German federal system, but warned "you must not underestimate the political symbol this would give. That a single party, and a right-wing party, could rule a German state… The symbol that these parties, that have been ruling Germany since 1949 or the East since 1990, they now lose control. They now lose power. I think this is a much more important symbol than just saying, OK, (the) AfD will change this or that in its local school system or university system."

Schatz described the AfD "a nationalist, anti-immigration party on the far right that has become a powerful vehicle for voter anger at Germany’s political establishment — especially in the former East Germany. It campaigns for much tighter immigration, a stronger emphasis on German national identity, rejection of much of the green agenda and a softer line toward Russia."

An outright win for the AfD, even in Germany’s sixth smallest state, would break through the political establishment’s so-called "Brandmauer," or "firewall." Simply put, other parties refuse to work with the AfD, which is currently the second-largest party in the Bundestag, officially the opposition party, after winning 20.8% of the vote in the February 2025 federal election.
'SEND THEM BACK' CHANTS ROCK EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AFTER LANDSLIDE VOTE TO SPEED UP DEPORTATIONS
The AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, campaigns during the 2026 state election in Saxony-Anhalt. (Sebastian Willnow/picture alliance via Getty Images)

In an interview on German broadcaster ZDF, the AfD’s national co-chair, Alice Weidel, advocated for closing Germany’s borders and exiting Europe’s Schengen treaty, saying, "Illegal migration, unchecked open borders, anyone can get in. Our internal security is suffering. People are honestly fed up with this situation."

Weidel added, "All Syrian refugees must have their protected status revoked because the reason for their flight no longer exists. These people must return to their homeland. If they don't leave voluntarily, then they must be deported by force." Adding that many of the 1.3 million Syrians in Germany are being naturalized, "we must stop naturalizing these people who should actually be leaving our country. We have Islamization."
GERMAN OFFICIALS WANT TO KNOW WHY BERLIN ATTACK SUSPECT WAS FREE DESPITE ALLEGED ISIS SUPPORT

Regional elections in the eastern federal state of Saxony-Anhalt will take place on Sept. 6, 2026, and two weeks later, the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the capital Berlin itself will also elect their state assemblies on Sept.20, 2026. (Ronny Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images)

In May 2025, Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" group, citing "anti-migrant positions and an ancestry-based definition of German identity." This past February, according to Deutsche Welle, that classification was put on hold by a German court after "Judges found that while there was evidence of potentially unconstitutional statements and policies within the AfD… it said that there was not sufficient evidence to characterize the party as a whole as extremist."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently told state broadcaster ARD, "I cannot imagine international investors attending a ground-breaking ceremony with an AfD Minister-President to set up new plants and establish new businesses in Saxony-Anhalt… However, that is a decision for ​the voters in Saxony-Anhalt to make. The state will suffer ⁠considerable damage if things turn out as we now fear they ​might."
This has done little to damage the popularity of the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund. In a state of just over 2 million people, he has a TikTok following of over 700,000.

A Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS) report said Siegmund’s "polished appearance and professional tone lend respectability, and radical demands blend with footage of a community-oriented politician responding to audience questions… The AfD’s physical presence in the streets and omnipresence in the media helps to push the common populist ‘us versus them’ narrative: The AfD is here for you, the other parties are not."
NEW GERMANY SEX-CRIME FIGURES REIGNITE MIGRATION FIGHT AS EXPLOITATION PROBE EXPANDS
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sparked backlash while remarking about the country's migration policies. (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)

According to the independent, non-partisan German website Wahlrecht.de, which tracks federal and state election polling, ahead of Sunday’s vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD holds a 41%-23% lead over the CDU, followed by three leftist parties. A party or a coalition needs at least half of the seats to control parliament and name a state minister-president, essentially a governor. So how can a party with only 43% win an election outright? That comes down to Germany’s unique election system.

"German voters cast two ballots," Schatz says, "One for a local candidate — like voting for your congressman — and one for a party. That second vote, the party vote, is the one that counts. It decides how many seats each party gets in parliament." But there is a caveat: "Any party that falls below 5% gets nothing — zero seats — and those votes are effectively thrown out. Right now, several smaller parties are hovering right at that line. If they miss it, 42% or 43% of the vote can translate into more than half the seats. So Saxony-Anhalt could wake up to an AfD majority government even though a clear majority of voters chose someone else. That would be a first in postwar Germany."

The CSIS report said voters are drawn to the AfD "because, or despite of, its extremist ideology. 60.5% of AfD voters hold a right-wing extremist worldview… At the same time, more than two in five AfD voters think that the party does not sufficiently distance itself from right-wing extremist positions." The report also found that AfD’s "strongest recent gains have been among voters 18 to 25 years old, where the party tripled its results compared to the 2021 national election."

Treiber said economics is pushing younger voters to the AfD, due to rising expenses and unemployment. He also said younger voters are "kind of polarized because the other part of the youth in Germany is voting for the left party (Die Linke)."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Saxony-Anhalt may just be the beginning for the anti-establishment parties. Voters in neighboring Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where former Chancellor Angela Merkel grew up and began her political career, go to the polls in two weeks. Polling data from Wahlrecht.de shows the AfD leading the ruling SPD 35%-32% there.

Conversely, in Berlin, where voters in the capital also go to the polls in two weeks, the average of recent polling has the far-left Die Linke in a dead heat with the CDU at 20%, followed by the AfD at 18%, with the Greens and the SPD each around 15%. While the majority of the AfD’s support does come from the former East Germany, the party is represented in 14 of Germany’s 16 state legislatures and holds 15 of Germany’s 96 seats in the European Parliament.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Fighter jet crashes at air show, killing 2 pilots with thousands of spectators watching
summary: Video captured a Phantom F-4 jet crashing into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver at Tanagra Air Force Base as thousands witnessed it.
story: A Greek air force fighter jet crashed and burst into flames during an air show with thousands of spectators. (Credit: @sovva1_1 via Storyful and REUTERS).
A day at an air show turned fatal Saturday when a Greek air force jet crashed north of Athens as thousands of spectators watched.
Both pilots were killed in the crash at Tanagra Air Force Base, but no civilians were hurt.
The twin-seat Phantom F-4 jet flew into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver just meters above the ground.
EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE

Spectators watch as smoke rises after a Hellenic Air Force F-4 Phantom fighter jet crashed during the Athens Flying Week airshow at Tanagra Air Force Base, north of Athens, Greece, Saturday. (AP Photo/Kallista Allaway)

"The sense of grief is widespread, and our thoughts are with the families of the two pilots we lost," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said. "It is a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greece’s aviators, who remain on constant standby to protect Greece's skies."
The jet burst into flames on impact, sending up a large plume of black smoke, prompting 11 water-dropping planes and helicopters to assist 85 firefighters in extinguishing the blaze.
11 SKYDIVERS, ONE PILOT KILLED IN MISSOURI PLANE CRASH NEAR AIRPORT
Video of the crash showed a second ball of fire nearby as the plane broke apart.
The bodies of the pilots were eventually recovered.
Smoke rises after a Hellenic Air Force F-4 Phantom fighter jet crashed during the Athens Flying Week airshow at Tanagra Air Force Base, north of Athens, Greece, Saturday. (AP Photo/undefined)
"We were all stunned. It hadn't been airborne for more than three minutes," an eyewitness told ERT, Greece’s state-owned broadcaster.
The crash happened during the country’s annual Athens Flying Week.
The organizers canceled the rest of the events after the incident, and the area was evacuated.
Two pilots were killed in the crash. (Reuters)

"It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base," Cyprus' Defense Minister Vasilis Palmas said, adding he had called Nikos Dendias, Greece’s Minister of National Defense.
AIR FORCE IDENTIFIES 8 CREW MEMBERS KILLED IN B-52 STRATOFORTRESS CRASH AT EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE
The air force has declared three days of mourning in the country.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In May, two jets collided during an air show in Idaho, but the pilots were able to safely eject.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: United Nations votes 164-1 for Equal Earth map after US brands it 'radical ideological project'
summary: The United Nations adopted the Equal Earth map showing Africa's true size, but the United States was the sole nation to vote against the resolution.
story: Yaryna Ferencevych, the deputy U.S. representative to the United Nations, voted against changing the official map of the world to reflect Africa's true size.
The United Nations on Friday was one vote shy of unanimously adopting a new map of the world that shows Africa's true size, making the continent appear far larger than it does on traditional maps.

The United States was the only one of 165 member nations to vote against the U.N. General Assembly resolution to accept the Equal Earth map projection, which depicts countries and continents in their true relative sizes, according to the map creator's website.
Six nations abstained, including Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine.

Yaryna Ferencevych, the deputy U.S. representative to the U.N. Economic and Social Council, said the resolution was presented as "an anodyne effort to update cartographic proportions" but was, in her view, part of a "much larger and more radical ideological project."

Yaryna Ferencevych, the deputy U.S. representative to the United Nations Economic and Social Council, speaks against adopting the Equal Earth world map during the 114th plenary meeting of the 80th session of the U.N. General Assembly Sept. 4, 2026. (United Nations)
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION REJECTS UN MIGRATION DECLARATION, SAYS 'MASS MIGRATION WAS NEVER SAFE'

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," Ferencevych said Friday during the 114th Plenary meeting.
"Resolutions like this one and the ideological agenda they promote are barnacles on our work here and the reason this institution is losing its credibility."

Ferencevych was referring to the Mercator projection, created in 1569 to aid maritime navigation. To this day, it is seen as the traditional world map and is used in many school textbooks and atlases.
It enlarges land masses near the poles and reduces the apparent size of those near the equator, making Africa appear far smaller relative to Greenland and Europe than it is in reality.
The Equal Earth map that the United Nations favors. It depicts all continents at their true sizes relative to one another. (Courtesy: Tom Patterson)
AFRICAN AND CARIBBEAN LEADERS CALL FOR PAYMENTS, DEBT CANCELLATION, FORMAL APOLOGIES OVER SLAVERY

Togo Foreign Minister Robert Dussey, who introduced the resolution on behalf of the African Group, said adopting the new map would "promote projections that better preserve the true proportions of continents."

"A fair map does not change the geography of the world; it changes how we see the world," he said. "And when our perspective becomes more just, it paves the way for greater understanding, respect and peace among nations."
The measure does not require countries or companies to abandon the Mercator projection, but it establishes the U.N.'s official backing for equal-area maps as the preferred way to depict the world.
The world on Mercator projection between 85°3'4"S and 85°3'4"N. (Strebe)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Mercator projection largely fell out of favor among cartographers in the 20th century because of its distortions. However, it saw a resurgence after Google Maps adopted the Web Mercator projection in 2005, with virtually every major online mapping service following suit.

Web Mercator became the standard for online maps because it allowed for smooth panning and zooming across the globe, making it well suited for interactive digital maps, according to a 2014 Cartographica study.
The United States Mission to the United Nations and the ECOSOC did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Trump negotiators Witkoff, Kushner meet with Putin in Moscow as US pushes for end to Russia-Ukraine war
summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow for peace talks before heading to Kyiv, and President Donald Trump says there may be a good chance for a deal.
story: Russian President Vladimir Putin greets U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin on Saturday for talks on ending Russia's war with Ukraine. (The Associated Press)

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law and advisor, Jared Kushner, met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin in Moscow on Saturday, as part of a weekend journey that will take them to Kyiv on Sunday in an effort to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin for more than three hours behind closed doors, The Associated Press reported, and concluded without any breakthroughs.
The AP said Putin’s foreign policy advisor, Yuri Ushakov, called the talks constructive, frank and useful.

"Today, Special Envoy Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with President Vladimir Putin of Russia to advance President Trump's agenda of peace in the Russia-Ukraine War. They were joined by officials from the National Security Council, State Department, and Treasury Department to discuss proposals to bring peace to this conflict," a White House official said after Saturday's talks. "The American delegation also thanked President Putin for releasing former United States Marine Robert Gilman from Russian custody out of respect for President Trump.
"The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES SURPRISE THREE-DAY CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

President Vladimir Putin, right, greets U.S. envoys Jared Kushner, left, and Steve Witkoff, center, prior to talks at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin in Moscow, on Saturday. (Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)
On Friday, Trump addressed Saturday's anticipated visit with reporters.

"We have an idea for peace. I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators," he said. "They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it."
Kushner and Witkoff visited Russia first on Saturday, and were greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev shortly after landing in Moscow.
Kushner and Witkoff will be Kyiv on Sunday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelenskyy.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine will work to keep Russian airspace safe during the Americans’ visit.
CIA DIRECTOR JOHN RATCLIFFE MET WITH RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE OFFICIALS IN VISIT TO MOSCOW, KREMLIN SAYS

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff, right, Jared Kushner, center, and Presidential Envoy Kirill Dmitriev stand prior to talks at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin in Moscow, on Saturday. (Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)

"Just as we did during previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are looking out for them, not for Russia. There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit," Zelenskyy wrote.

"Our goal is to make the visit and the talks with the U.S. side as constructive and substantive as possible. We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end. We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response."
ZELENSKYY CONGRATULATES TRUMP ON TURNING 80 IN BIRTHDAY CALL, VOWS MORE UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AT G7 ON TUESDAY
Zelenskyy’s message Friday came the same day a Russian drone strike targeted the Security Service of Ukraine’s headquarters in Ukraine. (@ZelenskyyUa via X)
Zelenskyy, in a subsequent Saturday morning post on X, said he had already communicated with Witkoff and Kushner ahead of their planned Sunday meeting.

"I have just spoken with the U.S. President’s envoys. They have already begun working with the Russian side today. From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process. From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv," Zelenskyy wrote.

"Today, I also received reports from Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi on the situation at the front, the dynamics of threats in Ukraine’s airspace, our steps, and active defensive operations. I am grateful to every one of our warriors for effectively defending Ukraine’s positions," Zelenskyy's post continued.

"On the diplomatic track, our actions must be, and will be, just as strong and effective – one hundred percent. The plan for tomorrow’s diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the U.S. team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation. Thank you to everyone who stands with Ukraine!"
PUTIN UNLEASHES NEW FURY ON UKRAINE AS REPORT EXPOSES FEAR HANGING OVER WAR’S END

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, right, greets U.S. special representatives Jared Kushner, center, and Steve Witkoff upon their arrival Saturday at Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow, Russia. (Reuters)
Zelenskyy’s message Friday came the same day a Russian drone strike targeted the Security Service of Ukraine’s headquarters in Ukraine, Zelenskyy wrote in a public message on the app Telegram.
Zelenskyy alleged the strike directly targeted the head of the Security Service's office.
He also wrote that he was directing the head, Oleksandr Poklad, to prepare a retaliatory strike.

"I gave Poklad the task of adequately, noticeably and, if possible, mirroring the Russians' response to this attack, when everything is prepared. Our military will support this response. Glory to Ukraine!" Zelenskyy wrote.
At least nine people were injured in the explosion, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also wrote on Telegram.
RUSSIA’S STRIKES NEAR MOLDOVA RAISE ALARM OVER PUTIN’S PLANS FOR EUROPE’S EASTERN FLANK

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, center, walks with U.S. special representatives Jared Kushner, left, and Steve Witkoff upon their arrival Saturday at Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow, Russia. (Reuters)
The visit also comes just one day after German officials formally accused Russia of attempting an explosive drone attack on a major airport in Germany.

"The attack on the aircraft in Leipzig was concrete; it could have triggered a catastrophe had it succeeded. The attacker was, at most, covert, but even here there is now certainty: The German government has named Russia as the mastermind. Patterns of attack, police investigations, and intelligence findings prove Russian responsibility for the drone attack," Stefan Kornelius, a spokesperson for the German federal government, wrote Friday.
Fox News Digital contacted the White House and the foreign ministries for Russia, Ukraine and Germany for further comment.

title: Russia's shadow war is putting Europe on edge as Germany confronts a growing threat
summary: Germany accused Russia of a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and now pushes Baltic Sea allies to form a rapid-response hybrid warfare task force.
story: Jennifer Griffin reports on Russia's shadow fleet launching a drone campaign across Europe to surveil military sites and test NATO's air defenses. The International Institute for Strategic Studies report reveals 144 suspected drones near sensitive sites in Germany, France, and the UK.

Germany is pushing European partners to create a rapid-response task force in the Baltic Sea region as Berlin confronts what it says is an escalating campaign of Russian hybrid warfare, including an attempted explosives-laden drone attack on one of the country's most important cargo airports.

The initiative, proposed by German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt following an Aug. 28 meeting in Flensburg, is intended to allow Baltic Sea countries to rapidly exchange information and coordinate responses to hybrid threats ranging from drones and sabotage to cyberattacks, disinformation and attacks on critical infrastructure.
"We want to turn this shared threat environment into a shared security environment," Dobrindt said, warning that hybrid threats were becoming more frequent and sophisticated.
The proposal has taken on new urgency after Germany formally accused Russia this week of responsibility for an attempted Aug. 4 attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport involving a drone carrying explosives.
EXPLOSIVE DRONE FORCES SHUTDOWN AT MAJOR GERMAN AIRPORT SERVING NATO, UKRAINE FLIGHTS

A drone carrying explosives was found at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport on Tuesday night next to a Ukrainian plane, with officials warning the incident represented "a new quality of danger." (Hendrik Schmidt/DPA via AP)

German officials said police findings, intelligence information and the methods used in the attack led Berlin to conclude Russia was responsible. The government said aspects of the drone, explosives and detonation technology were consistent with methods seen in previous Russian hybrid operations and in Moscow's war against Ukraine.

Germany has not publicly released much of the underlying evidence, saying details including information about suspected perpetrators, travel routes, surveillance footage and DNA evidence are being withheld to protect the investigation.
Latvia characterized the Leipzig attack in even stronger terms.

"The attack in Leipzig confirms once again that Russia poses a direct threat to the security of all of Europe. This was not merely a hybrid attack, but state-sponsored terrorism on German soil," Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said in a statement published by Latvia's Foreign Ministry.
Braže also called for continued efforts to strengthen Ukraine's defense capabilities and for additional sanctions aimed at limiting Russia's ability to produce missiles, drones and other weapons.
US INTEL WARNS RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH LIMITED ATTACK ON NATO ALLY IN EFFORT TO FRAGMENT ORGANIZATION: REPORT

Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev, attends an event in Berlin in May. Germany summoned Nechayev after accusing Moscow of carrying out the failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. (Christoph Soeder/Picture Alliance via Getty Images, File)
Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital that the episode reflects what he described as a widening pattern of hostile activity.

"We are clearly seeing an escalation in the scope and intensity of Russian gray-zone hostile actions across Europe," Newton said. "Russia has long used a variety of non-military, covert, and hybrid tactics – cyberattacks, information operations, sabotage, other covert means – to create disruption while staying just below the threshold of open conflict with NATO."
Newton called Germany's attribution of the Leipzig plot "particularly serious," saying it "demonstrates how dangerous these operations are becoming."

Germany responded by announcing the closure of Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the arrangement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin. Berlin also said it would tighten entry controls for Russian nationals and increase pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet.
Russia has denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling Germany's accusations "entirely fabricated" and accusing Berlin of escalating tensions, according to Reuters.
The heightened concern comes as German police separately investigate a cluster of suspected sabotage incidents targeting the country's electricity infrastructure this week.
REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

Polish soldiers stand watch near the Belarus border, where officials say migration pressure has evolved into a form of hybrid warfare targeting NATO’s eastern flank. May 16th, 2026. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
Authorities were investigating a suspicious device found near a substation in Dormagen, North Rhine-Westphalia, on Friday, following incidents in Bergheim and Brandenburg.
In Bergheim, deliberate interference temporarily forced lignite-fired generating units representing about 4,200 megawatts of capacity offline, though no broader blackout occurred.
German authorities have not publicly connected those power-grid incidents to Russia, a distinction Newton said was important.
"We need to be careful when attributing these hostile acts and ensure we have indisputable intelligence information that clearly leads to the source of these belligerent actions," Newton said.
"The incidents involving Germany’s power infrastructure are still under investigation and have not been publicly attributed to Russia, or any other source for that matter," he added.
The German government nevertheless said Friday that the country faces a persistent hybrid threat.
"Germany is not at war, but it is a daily target of hybrid warfare," the government said, citing attacks on communications systems, disinformation and arson targeting the defense industry.
EUROPE BANKROLLS PUTIN'S WAR MACHINE EVEN AS NATO RACES TO BOLSTER DEFENSES
NATO Chiefs of Defense hold a hybrid meeting with screens showing allied leaders joining remotely, Aug. 20 2025. (NATO)

Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital that Moscow has increasingly sought to pressure Western countries while avoiding conventional conflict.

"We do know that Russia is trying to fight the Western world below the line of kinetic conflict and their methods are getting ever bolder, whether through cyber operations, sabotage, drones and other forms of pressure across Europe," Breedlove said. "We’re even becoming aware of things they are doing inside the United States."
Breedlove said Russian President Vladimir Putin has long sought to exploit divisions within NATO, "especially between the United States and Europe."
"The Western world has got to step up to counter the Russian threat," he said.

The Baltic initiative comes amid broader efforts by NATO and regional governments to protect an area increasingly associated with threats to undersea cables, pipelines, shipping and other critical infrastructure.
NATO already operates Baltic Sentry, an enhanced vigilance activity launched in 2025 to strengthen protection of critical undersea infrastructure in the Baltic Sea.

In February, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden agreed to accelerate the acquisition and integration of new technologies for Baltic naval operations. NATO said that initiative built on testing involving roughly 70 aerial and maritime drones in 2025.
Breedlove said Germany's proposed task force could help bridge intelligence, law-enforcement and military responses among regional partners.

"Germany’s Baltic initiative makes sense," he said. "The value is also for partner countries to share information faster, connect the intelligence, law-enforcement and military pieces, and make decisions before Russia can take advantage of confusion or delay."
Newton similarly said the task force could complement NATO's existing military activity by improving governments' ability to rapidly share intelligence and coordinate security responses.
Breedlove warned that Moscow would continue searching for opportunities to exploit uncertainty.

BALTIC SEA (June 5, 2025) The Blue Ridge-class command and control ship USS Mount Whitney (LCC 20) participates in exercise Baltic Operations 2025 (BALTOPS 25) as ships sail in formation through the Baltic Sea, June 5, 2025. BALTOPS 25, the premiere maritime-focused exercise in the Baltic Region, provides a unique training opportunity to strengthen combined response capabilities critical to preserving freedom of navigation and security in the Baltic Sea. (U.S. Navy Courtesy Photo)

"Without question, the Russians will keep looking for places where they can create uncertainty and hesitation," he said. "We need to get better at recognizing their actions with speed – and responding forcefully with the strength of our allies."

Fox News Digital reached out to the German Embassy in Washington, D.C., and the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment but did not receive responses by publication time.

Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. title: From cockroach milk to stepping on snakes, Ig Nobel awards celebrates science at its oddest
summary: Cockroach milk, kissing evolution and the underwear soil test were among the unusual real studies honored at the Ig Nobel ceremony in Zurich.
story: An Arkansas high school football player discovered a cottonmouth snake inside his helmet after completing a practice. Animal control was able to remove the two-foot reptile from the padding after he wore the equipment during practice.

A motley crew of scientists was honored this week for its unusual contributions, which included studying cockroach milk, the evolutionary history of kissing and testing soil health by using underwear.
The satirical Ig Nobel ceremony, which honors unusual but real studies, took place in Zurich Thursday and was presented by the digital magazine, the Annals of Improbable Research.
The awards, which were founded in 1991, took place outside the U.S. for the first time this year over the concern that the honorees wouldn’t be able to get a visa.

Other winners included researchers who found upper-class people were more likely to engage in unethical behavior, such as stealing candy from a baby, a study on proper nose blowing and gently stepping on snakes to see what provokes them into biting people.
WASHINGTON HOMEOWNER HEARS MYSTERIOUS BANGING CALLS 911 BEFORE POLICE FIND GROWLING BOBCAT AT TOP OF STAIRS

Soil Science Prize winners Pia Viviani, right, and Atlant Bieri, left, stand on stage during the Ig Nobel Prize ceremony at the Zurich Convention Center in Zurich, Switzerland, Thursday. (Claudio Thoma/Keystone via AP)

"The general pattern seems to be that, with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships," Dr. Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine said, according to the Guardian.
"Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries, but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritize one’s own needs over those of others."

The final four honorees included those studying the power of having mutual enemies, attempts at a splash-free urinal, using dead mosquitos for 3D printing and research that found parents love the smell of their newborn babies but not teenage children.

In case you’re wondering, the team studying the history of kissing has defined it as "a non-agonistic interaction involving directed, intraspecific, oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer." Romantic.

From left, Nobel Prize winners Esther Duflo, Abhijit Banerjee, Michel Mayor and Tim Hunt look at underwear handed over by the Soil Science Award winners during the Ig Nobel Prize ceremony at the Zurich Convention Center in Zurich, Switzerland, Thursday. (Claudio Thoma/Keystone via AP)
COUPLE PUBLICLY CANED AFTER ALLEGED TIKTOK KISS SPARKS OUTRAGE IN INDONESIA

"Next time you kiss someone, you can think, 'This is a 21.5 million-year-old tradition that I'm honoring here," evolutionary biologist Matilda Brindle of the University of Oxford said, according to NPR. "It's not just a modern human behavior. It's really ancestral.' And to us, that suggests that it probably has quite a useful evolutionary function."
Brindle said her team believes that Neanderthals not only kissed each other. They may have also kissed early humans.
CAVE DISCOVERY PUSHES BACK EVIDENCE OF HUMAN ANCESTORS USING FIRE TO 1.79M YEARS AGO
The winners of the Ig Nobel Prize pose for a group picture during the ceremony at the Zurich Convention Center in Zurich, Switzerland, Thursday. (Claudio Thoma/Keystone via AP)
All the honorees receive a trophy that looks like a cross between a mushroom and a human foot while the audience throws paper airplanes at them.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Ig Nobel has no relation to the actual Nobel Prize, which will announce its honorees in October.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trapped Nepal workers pulled alive from tunnel 9 days after deadly flooding, raising hope for more rescues
summary: Two workers were pulled alive from a Nepal hydropower tunnel nine days after catastrophic floods, and one rescued man says more people are trapped inside.
story: On Friday morning, searchers heard men's voices, which prompted an all-out rescue mission with the help of the Nepal Army. (Credit: Nepali Army via Storyful)
Rescue teams in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after catastrophic floods swept through the country, leaving more than 1,000 people dead and thousands more missing.

Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane told The Associated Press that searchers first heard men's voices in the tunnel on Friday morning. Images distributed by the Nepal Army showed a rescuer carrying one of the workers on his back while soldiers on either side helped.

The breakthrough has raised hopes that the dozens of others believed to be trapped will be rescued. One of the rescued men said more people are alive inside the tunnel, according to Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, who said the search is ongoing.
SON REALIZES MISSING AMERICAN DAD WAS IN PATH OF NEPAL DISASTER AFTER WATCHING VIRAL VIDEO
Soldiers rescue a worker alive from a tunnel during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa district on Sept. 4, 2026. (Nepal Army via AP)
"I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God," Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of those rescued, told the AP.
Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, and one of them was in critical condition, the AP reported, citing a statement from the prime minister's office.
Officials identified them as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor at the Trishuli 3A plant.
On Sept. 4, 2026, a rescuer carried one of the workers who was trapped for days in the tunnel at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project. Soldiers flank him on either side. (Nepal Army via AP)
TERRIFYING VIDEO CAPTURES PEOPLE FLEEING INCOMING MUDSLIDE AT NEPAL-CHINA BORDER
The AP reported that about 115 people are believed to remain trapped in the Trishuli 3A tunnel alone, citing the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
In total, authorities say there are about 900 workers missing from 12 hydropower plants in Nepal, with about 500 of them believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page that officials "are waiting for the rescue of more and more people."
"A heartfelt thank you to everyone who worked tirelessly day and night to rescue two people alive!" Timilsina added.
One of the workers, covered in mud, is lifted out of the tunnel by rescue teams on Sept. 4, 2026. (Nepal Army via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The AP reported that at least 1,287 people have been killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after the Aug. 26 floods, which scientists believe were likely triggered by a glacier collapse.
China said on Wednesday that on the Tibet side of the border, 21 people were killed and 541 are missing.
Nepal's disaster agency chief told Reuters on Friday that the flooding has likely caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees (about $2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: US adversary turns up the heat on America’s AI lead with an underestimated edge
summary: China's "East Data, West Computing" initiative is rapidly expanding AI infrastructure, but a major chip constraint complicates Beijing's push.
story: China expert Gordon Chang discusses why he believes Beijing is looking to exploit US opposition to new data centers as China works to narrow America’s lead in AI infrastructure.

China is racing to build the data centers and energy infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence, raising concerns that Beijing’s ability to rapidly construct massive projects could help it get closer to America’s commanding lead in the physical infrastructure underpinning the AI race.

The U.S. remains far ahead in sheer numbers. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence’s 2026 AI Index, using Cloudscene data, counted 5,427 U.S. data centers in 2025 compared with 449 in China. Stanford cautioned that the count does not account for differences in facility size, computing capacity or utilization.
But China is moving quickly.
AMERICA IS FIGHTING YESTERDAY’S AI WAR. TOMORROW’S WAR IS ON THE WAY
People visit the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, China, July 18, 2026. (Go Nakamura/Reuters)
"We know that China is far behind, but we also know that they are moving at great speed," China expert Gordon Chang told Fox News Digital.

Chang argued that Beijing understands the U.S. advantage will be difficult to erase if America continues building at the same pace and said growing opposition to data-center development could slow that expansion.
President Donald Trump made a similar argument this week, warning communities fighting new projects that China stands to benefit.

"China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!" Trump also argued that communities embracing data centers would gain jobs and tax revenues.
Vice President JD Vance sharpened that warning Thursday, telling FOX Business there was "a very good chance" the U.S. could lose the AI race to China if Democrats regain control of Congress.

Vance said the broader problem is America’s ability to build enough power to support data centers and other major infrastructure. "We cannot be a country that says we’re not going to build more power," Vance said, arguing that the administration is trying to make it easier to construct power plants alongside data centers while protecting residential ratepayers from higher electricity costs.
AI BOOM: DEMAND FOR DATA CENTERS DRIVES INNOVATION BY ENERGY, TECH INDUSTRIES TO PRODUCE NEW POWER SOURCES

He also pointed to the widening U.S.-China electricity gap, saying China now generates roughly three times as much power as the United States. "We’ve got to build more power plants. We’ve got to make the regulatory state easier to work with."
Asked about China’s rapid infrastructure expansion, the Chinese Embassy in Washington rejected the premise that AI should primarily be viewed as a geopolitical contest.
"AI should not be owned by major countries, still less dominated by contests and rivalry," Embassy spokesperson Liu Chang told Fox News Digital.

Liu pointed to China’s 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan, which calls for accelerating construction of clean power, next-generation networks, computing capacity and data centers. He said China advocates cooperation with the U.S. and wants AI development to benefit both countries and the broader international community.
Behind that diplomatic message, Beijing is undertaking a massive geographic reorganization of its computing infrastructure.

Under China’s "East Data, West Computing" initiative, Beijing is directing more computing capacity toward western regions where land is available and wind and solar resources can help reduce energy costs.

Five of China’s eight national computing hubs are located in western China, according to a June 25 report from the government-backed Digital China initiative. More than 30 data centers were under construction within a three-kilometer area in Horinger, Inner Mongolia, while intensive construction was also underway in Zhongwei, Ningxia.
Huawei Technology Co.'s new data center is seen under construction in Guian New Zone, in southwestern China's Guizhou province May 14, 2019. Picture taken May 14, 2019. (Reuters)
That buildout caught the attention of members of the bipartisan US-China Economic and Security Review Commission during a recent fact-finding trip to China.

"I left with an intense belief that the Chinese see this as the frontier in terms of competition," Commission Vice Chairman Mike Kuiken told Fox News Digital, describing AI as increasingly intertwined with robotics, biotechnology, advanced materials and manufacturing.
Kuiken said China has one significant advantage when it comes to constructing the infrastructure needed to support that technology.
"The Chinese, because they write the rules as they go, and the rule of law largely does not exist, are able to just move faster in terms of building things," he said.
But Kuiken also identified a major Chinese weakness: access to the most advanced chips.

"The constraints that are real though, the Chinese do not have the ability to procure advanced chips," he said, while describing Beijing’s ability to rapidly construct coal plants and other infrastructure as "quite incredible."
THE WAR ON DATA CENTERS JEOPARDIZES OUR ECONOMY AND NATIONAL SECURITY
The AI boom is accelerating demand for data centers across Texas as companies seek more space, power and infrastructure to support increasingly intensive computing needs. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The U.S. retains major advantages beyond its data-center lead. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence’s 2026 AI Index found that America produced 59 notable AI models in 2025 compared with 35 from China, and U.S. private AI investment reached $285.9 billion, compared with $12.4 billion in China. Stanford cautioned that private investment figures understate Beijing’s overall spending because of Chinese government-backed funds.
At the same time, Chinese models have rapidly narrowed the performance gap. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index found that as of March 2026, the top U.S. model led the top Chinese model by just 2.7%.

Chang also alleged that Beijing is seeking to exploit American opposition to data centers and claimed China-linked networks have helped support protests against projects in the US. "These protests are not entirely organic," Chang told Fox News Digital.

Kuiken was cautious about portraying those local disputes as part of a broader anti-China fight, saying genuine U.S. opposition to data-center projects has also emerged over concerns including electricity costs, water use, noise and land development.

"We are building things in the U.S. faster than we have in a long time," he said, adding that policymakers are working through infrastructure constraints. "Usually there are local issues that are driving those things."
The emerging competition, therefore, is not simply over who develops the smartest AI model.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Robots fight during an MMA-style performance at Engine AI booth at the 2026 World Robot Conference, in Beijing, China, August 19, 2026. (Maxim Shemetov/Reuters)
It is increasingly a race over who can build the electricity, data centers, chips and networks needed to run those models at enormous scale — and how quickly they can build them.

She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. title: New Hampshire primaries test Trump and the left
summary: Trump has backed former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the Senate primary, in which Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas faces a democratic socialist.
story: President Donald Trump’s endorsement will be put to the test once again Tuesday in New Hampshire’s primaries, where liberal Democrats are also looking to cap an ascendant primary season with additional victories.
Granite State voters are among the last in the country to choose nominees for November’s elections, and Tuesday’s contests will set the matchup in one of this year’s most competitive Senate races.

Trump is hoping his preferred candidate, former GOP Sen. John Sununu, prevails in the primary. On the Democratic side, Rep. Chris Pappas is looking to fend off a democratic socialist opponent for his party’s Senate nomination.
A divisive Democratic battle is also unfolding in one of the state’s competitive House seats, which Pappas left open, while another House Democrat is facing a primary challenger from the left.
Here’s what to watch Tuesday in New Hampshire, where poll closing times vary by municipality, ranging from 7 to 8 p.m. ET.
Senate matchup
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s retirement opened up this Senate seat, and Republicans are hoping to make the race competitive in November.

Pappas, who has won in a battleground seat since 2018, is considered the front-runner for his party’s nomination. He already appears to be gearing up for the general election, focusing his campaign on addressing high costs and political corruption and already launching an ad attacking a potential Republican opponent.

But Pappas is facing a challenge from the left from Karishma Manzur, a scientist and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who supports progressive policies like “Medicare for All.” Manzur has sharply criticized Pappas over support and funding for Israel, saying he is “enabling genocide.”

The GOP primary includes multiple candidates, but the race is largely between Sununu and another former senator, Scott Brown, who held a Massachusetts seat for three years, previously ran for the New Hampshire Senate in 2014 and served as Trump’s ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during the president’s first term.
But the president backed Sununu, who also has support from Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

Sununu represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 through 2008 after serving in the House. He lost his bid for re-election in 2008 to Shaheen, but Republicans believe his well-known family name could give him a boost: Sununu’s brother and father both served as governors.

Trump lost the Granite State by just 3 points in 2024, giving Republicans hope about making this open-seat race competitive two years later. The GOP has not won a Senate race there since 2010, but New Hampshire does have a Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte.
Ayotte is running for a second two-year term as one of two GOP governors up for re-election in a state Trump lost two years ago. Ayotte is not facing any major primary challengers.

The Democratic nominee is all but certain to be former New Hampshire Executive Council member Cinde Warmington, who also faces no major competitors and unsuccessfully sought her party’s gubernatorial nomination in 2024.
House battles
The Democratic Party’s divides are on full display in a primary in Pappas’ now-open seat in the 1st District, which includes Manchester, the state’s biggest city.

A crowded field of candidates is running in both parties’ primaries, and the race could be competitive in the fall. Pappas won re-election by 8 points in 2024, but then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried the district by just 2 points.

Two of the front-runners are viewed as the most establishment Democrats: Marine veteran Maura Sullivan, the former congressional candidate and former Defense Department official, and Stefany Shaheen, a health advocate, former Portsmouth City Council member and daughter of the retiring senator. Over the weekend, Army National Guard officer Christian Urrutia, who had been running as a progressive, ended his campaign and backed Shaheen.

Another top contender in the race is progressive Carleigh Beriont, a union organizer. Heath Howard, who was backed by the local Democratic Socialists of America chapter, is still on the ballot but dropped out of the race and endorsed Beriont.

On the Republican side, Trump and other Republican leaders have endorsed auto businessman Anthony DiLorenzo. He is facing competition for the GOP nod from state Rep. Brian Cole and Hollie Noveletsky, a military veteran and CEO of her family iron company.
In the state’s other congressional district, Democratic Rep. Maggie Goodlander is facing a primary challenge from state Rep. Paige Beauchemin, a former nurse who entered politics in 2023.

The challenger is running as an unabashed progressive, calling for halting data center construction, new regulations on the artificial intelligence industry, “Medicare for All,” labeling Israel’s conduct in Gaza a “genocide” and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Although Beauchemin’s campaign is trying to tap into some of the progressive energy that has helped challengers topple incumbents this year, she has struggled to raise money — bringing in $44,000 to Goodlander’s $4.2 million — and hasn’t drawn any outside support from progressive groups.

Goodlander is a first-term lawmaker who recently gained national prominence as one of the national security-minded Democratic lawmakers who made a video telling the military that members could refuse illegal orders. She also worked in the Biden White House and Justice Department and is married to former Biden national security adviser Jake Sullivan. Lily Tang Williams, a former Colorado libertarian who since moved to the state, is expected to win the Republican nomination after she lost to Goodlander in 2024.

title: Supreme Court rejects Missouri Republicans’ request to use new congressional map
summary: Republicans rushed to the high court after the Missouri Supreme Court ruled the state could not use the redrawn map, which was designed to eliminate one Democratic-held seat, this year.
story: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected a last-ditch effort by Missouri Republicans to use a newly drawn congressional map, which was designed to maximize their political power, for this year’s midterm elections.

In a brief order issued by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, the court left in place a Missouri Supreme Court ruling last week that said the map could not be used while a ballot initiative that could lead to the redrawn map’s being tossed out by voters moves forward. Kavanaugh handles emergency requests that arise from Missouri.

The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave prompted by President Donald Trump, was designed to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

But the Supreme Court’s decision means the 2022 map, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, will be in place for the November general election, even though Missouri’s August primaries were held under the redrawn map.
The legal clash erupted after the 2025 redistricting plan was enacted.

A group called People Not Politicians Missouri, led by Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.
But Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters.

The Missouri Supreme Court found that Hoskins should not have rejected the plan, unanimously concluding there is nothing in state law that says redistricting plans are exempt from the referendum process.
The referendum petition was “legal, sufficient and timely,” the court found.
Under state law, whenever a proposed ballot initiative that overrides the Legislature is deemed valid, the law is automatically put on hold until after the people vote on it.

The court also said any confusion caused by its ruling was a result of Hoskins’ delay in deciding whether the referendum could move forward. Hoskins waited until the last minute to reject the proposal ahead of an Aug. 4 deadline and broke with the state’s typical process of putting a law facing a veto referendum on hold when enough signatures are submitted.

Hoskins argued at the Supreme Court that the state court ruling violated the U.S. Constitution’s elections clause, which he said delegates significant powers to state legislatures in overseeing elections. The Supreme Court rejected a similar argument in a redistricting case from North Carolina in 2023.

Hoskins’ lawyers told the justices that the state court ruling had created chaos because the new map was used in this year’s primary election. If the state has to revert to the old map, “hundreds of thousands of Missourians will see their votes in the primary election rendered pointless,” they wrote.
Lawyers for the referendum supporters said in court filings that Hoskins was seeking at the Supreme Court a “political victory to which he was never entitled under the Missouri Constitution.”

In May, the Supreme Court rejected a similar attempt by Democrats in Virginia who sought to revive their own congressional map that had been approved by voters. The Virginia Supreme Court had found legal flaws in the process that led to the referendum.

title: U.S. strikes Iranian tankers after attempted attacks on Navy warship
summary: They’re the latest tit-for-tat strikes as Washington and Tehran lurch back toward fighting during more than six months of war.
story: The U.S. military sank five Iranian tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in response to attempted attacks by the IRGC on an American warship, according to U.S. Central Command.

“CENTCOM forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, Sept. 8, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days,” U.S. Central Command said in a post on X. “The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed.”
Four of the tankers were attacked in the Gulf of Oman and one was hit near Kharg Island, according to CENTCOM.
“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM said in a statement.

A U.S. strike hit an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil terminal, which has been repeatedly threatened by President Donald Trump, according to the semiofficial Tasnim news agency.    The U.S. military hit a second tanker near the port city of Jask, according to Iranian state TV.

The strikes on the Iranian tankers Tuesday come after the IRGC attempted to hit an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer over the weekend, resulting in a U.S. response in which the U.S. sank one tanker and permanently disabled two more.
Iran threatened to target oil tankers in Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for the U.S. strikes on Tuesday.

“Following the actions of the American military in targeting several Iranian oil tankers, we warn all oil tanker crews in the areas around the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which are hosting these forces and are complicit in their actions, to immediately evacuate their vessels, whether they are at anchor or docked as they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy said in a statement posted by the semi-official Fars news agency.

The Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war, has become the key battleground in the conflict as both the U.S. and Iran have attacked tankers.

The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

title: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy as it attempts to restart in 2027
summary: LIV Golf, the Saudi-funded tour that once aimed to take over professional golf, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday as it attempts to restructure and restart what it called its “next chapter.”
story: LIV Golf, the Saudi-funded tour that once aimed to take over professional golf, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday as it attempts to restructure and restart what it called its “next chapter.”
LIV Golf Chief Executive Scott O’Neil said in a statement that he believed deeply in the future of the tour, which plans to “begin its new era in early 2027.”

“This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf — one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem,” O’Neil said. “We are excited about what lies ahead and yet, there is still much to accomplish in the months ahead.”

The bankruptcy filing in U.S. bankruptcy court in New Jersey comes five years after the tour launched with enormous fanfare and the financial backing of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, with ambitions no less than supplanting the PGA Tour as golf's pre-eminent tour.

LIV initially signed some of the sport’s biggest names, but its format — which included 54-hole tournaments and team competitions with names like "Crushers GC" — never caught on, and a proposed 2023 merger with the PGA Tour never became final.

Speculation about LIV Golf's future began in mid-April, fueled by unconfirmed reports of an “emergency summit” in New York City featuring LIV Golf’s top executives on the eve of a tour stop in Mexico City. The PIF — which had sunk a reported $5 billion into LIV — later announced it was rethinking its investment strategy, transitioning "from a period of rapid growth and acceleration to a new phase of sustained value creation."

With the PIF’s funding pulled, the league entered a summer of uncertainty, and eventually canceled its season-ending championship in August in Michigan. That same month, O'Neil said the tour had an agreement in place with a new lead investor, but did not disclose who it was. As part of its bankruptcy filing Tuesday, LIV announced in a statement that it is aiming to restart with the help of BC Partners. To help keep LIV running as it navigates the bankruptcy process, LIV said it received debtor-in-possession loan of $49.6 million from the Saudi Arabia PIF.

LIV’s filing listed its golfers as its largest creditors, with Jon Rahm ($7.47 million), Bryson DeChambeau ($5.76 million) Dustin Johnson ($5.48 million) and Cameron Smith ($4.85 million) listed as having the largest claims. The company estimated its assets are worth between $100 million and $500 million, and its liabilities between $500 million to $1 billion.

Almost immediately after its launching in 2021, LIV Golf drew criticism as “sportswashing,” an example of Saudi Arabia using high-profile investments into sports as a way to distract from the country’s human rights record, soften its image globally and build influence within the U.S.
“If sportswashing is going to increase my GDP by 1%, then we will continue doing sportswashing,” Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told Fox News in 2023.

Just as quickly, LIV drew the ire of the PGA Tour, the organizer of a majority of pro golf events, by signing many of the sport’s best-known players and past major champions such as Brooks Koepka, Bryson DeChambeau, Phil Mickelson and Dustin Johnson to lucrative contracts to play on its breakaway tour.

When the PGA Tour suspended players who had resigned their PGA membership to take part in LIV competitions, then LIV-CEO Greg Norman, the former star golfer, wrote a letter to the PGA Tour's commissioner complaining that it was a move to "intimidate players by bullying and threatening them."

In 2023, the PGA Tour and LIV Golf announced a surprise merger to end their court battles. The decision sparked investigations by U.S. senators and the Justice Department. In a hearing concerning the partnership of the former golf rivals, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said the hearing was “about how a brutal, repressive regime can buy influence, indeed even take over a cherished American institution to cleanse its public image.”

Entering its fifth season this year, LIV’s big ambitions and roster of big-name players took a hit, however, when Koepka and a second major champion, Patrick Reed, left the tour in January. (In the bankruptcy filing, Koepka is listed as a creditor, with a claim of $1.7 million.) Soon after, Koepka played in a PGA Tour event. The defections followed the PGA’s decision to offer a small number of players who had left for LIV a pathway to return to playing in PGA events.

Though LIV plans to re-emerge next year, it will need players to sign on and Rahm, a former Masters champion who is one of its biggest former names, was noncommittal this week when asked about his future.
“There’s a lot of things that could happen, and it’s one of those things where time’s gonna tell,” Rahm told the BBC.

title: U.S. agencies say top Chinese AI companies systematically copied American models
summary: In its most detailed accusation yet, the U.S. government has named six Chinese AI companies that it says copied American companies for their AI secrets.
story: In an alert published Tuesday, the FBI, the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said top Chinese AI companies have systematically mined cutting-edge AI models from American companies since 2024, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini and xAI’s Grok, to build their own.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

The practice, known as distillation, is widespread in the AI industry, though it is often against AI companies’ terms of service. American companies and government officials have increasingly alleged in recent months that Chinese models are built by distilling American ones.

The U.S. has accused China for years of stealing intellectual property from American companies. Tuesday’s report said the distillation campaign had come “likely with Chinese government awareness,” but it did not claim that China’s intelligence played a role.

The White House frequently describes the U.S. as racing China to develop the most cutting-edge AI. President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24. Officials from both governments have traded barbs in recent weeks over whether China has been inappropriately stealing AI trade secrets.

The report accused six of the leading Chinese AI developers: DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI. It goes into significant detail, including a long list alleging that certain Chinese models distilled specific topics, like “legal specialization optimization,” “agentic functions” and “coach/assistant capabilities,” from particular American models.
“The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the report said.

American companies have made scattered accusations of distillation since at least last year, when OpenAI said DeepSeek had “inappropriately” based its model on ChatGPT. In February, Google said it was inundated with attempts to clone Gemini but declined to name a suspect.

The report also includes a list of recommendations for U.S. companies, including doing a better job of verifying users who pay for subscription services to American models and comparing notes with one another about suspicious behavior. It also recommended, in certain cases, downgrading or altering responses to queries believed to be malicious.

In April, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, Michael Kratsios, circulated a memorandum to the heads of federal agencies highlighting Chinese distillation of American AI systems as a critical issue. He wrote that distillation allowed Chinese companies to freeload off American innovation and circumvent safety guardrails built into American systems.
In July, Kratsios declared on X that Moonshot had distilled Anthropic’s advanced Fable model to develop its Kimi K3 system.

“Legitimate AI distillation used to create smaller, more efficient models plays a vital role in this open innovation ecosystem,” Kratsios wrote, echoing language in his April memorandum. “However, large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary U.S. technology and undermining American research is unacceptable.”
